speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday morning last, July 13, the hon. member for Essex East asked me to comment on a press interview given by Mr. Ezra Benson, Secretary of Agriculture for the United States. The Canadian Press dispatch covering this first appeared, to my knowledge, in the Montreal Star of Monday evening. I have a copy of that report here, and I was surprised at some of the statements attributed to Mr. Benson in this dispatch. I communicated with him by telephone on Wednesday last in order to find out whether the report was accurate, and to find out exactly what he did say, as well as to discuss matters which were covered in the press dispatch.
Perhaps I had better read what the dispatch says:
However, he made It clear that he was deeply concerned over what he described as a rather restrictive attitude by the Canadian government in some farm products, particularly turkeys.
American turkey growers were "quite upset" over what amounted to a virtual Canadian embargo on turkey imports, he said. The U.S. now are trying to get Canada to relax curbs and Mr. Benson was hopeful something would be done soon.
On the telephone Mr. Benson said that he had not used the word "embargo" at any time, and did not think he had used the word "upset". What he did say was that he had just returned from Europe, he had told the reporter, and on his return had found some reports from United States turkey growers who were concerned about exports to Canada. I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the United States and ourselves have had some discussions on the subject of the turkey import control we have in effect in Canada, and I think that the United States is now reasonably happy with this situation.
In connection with our proposed deficiency payments on hogs the newspaper report

Inquiries of the Ministry states as follows, and this is as though it were quoting Mr. Benson:
The U.S. also was concerned over reports that the Canadian government was in the midst of turning its price support on hogs into a system of deficiency payments, covering farmers on their losses but letting them do all their own marketing.
Benson said this deficiency payments system may "greatly stimulate" Canadian hog production and provide a "real threat" to American hog producers competing against Canadian hogs in the American market.
"These Canadian hogs could depress our own markets," he said, adding that the U.S. had a heavy hog surplus of its own. American prices had been falling and the U.S. Agriculture Department had issued "warnings" to producers to limit production.
Mr. Benson told me that these were not his statements but that they were statements of farm organizations in the United States, particularly the American farm bureau, which had made representations to this effect to him; but that he did not make the statements to the reporter and that they should not be attributed to him. I explained to Mr. Benson that our deficiency payment plan, rather than stimulating hog production, would be likely to have the opposite effect and that it was designed to bring production and consumption more into balance in Canada.
The only other matter that was dealt with in this report was in connection with wheat, and the newspaper report ends by quoting Mr. Benson to this effect:
"I still think that Canadian production is too high," he said.
I pointed out to Mr. Benson that Canadian reduction in acreage was greater than United States reduction, taking any five-year period such as 1935-39 or 1940-45 and comparing it with the last four to five years and that as a result of our reduction in acreage the figure had come down from 28,726,000 acres in 1940 to 20,899,000 acres last year.
I think there is no question but that the Americans are in grave difficulties, as Mr. Benson has said on many occasions, over the amount of wheat that is being produced there. Of course we have had, as everyone knows, a considerable amount of difficulty over the production of wheat in this country. However, I do not think there is any serious difficulty between us in that regard. The report on the meeting which was held in Washington in May, which the Minister of Trade and Commerce made to the house, indicated that with regard to the disposal of these surplus stocks of wheat we are now in a very much better position than has ever been the case as far as consultation and co-ordination of the disposal programs are concerned.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is partly right. I explained the plans to a very large, serious and constructively-minded delegation that met with me in my office yesterday, together with six members of parliament from the surrounding area. I told them that present plans call for one 5,000-foot runway, but that the department is making a submission to treasury board recommending that the runway be extended to 6,000 feet. I am very hopeful that treasury board will pass that recommendation.
Regarding the matter of the former government's promise to build two runways, I explained to the delegation that it is the policy of this government when we build our airports to build one runway at a time, and as soon as it is demonstrated that one runway will be inadequate to handle the traffic which offers at the airport, then we are only too glad to build a second runway. I was interested also to learn in studying this matter that the promise made by the former government to build two runways at this airport was made just prior to the 1957 election, when the former government were making lavish promises in an attempt to avert the landslide which eventually overtook them.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON CANCELLATION OF CULLING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Trinity-Conception asked me a question relative to the regulations governing the culling of salted cod fish in Newfoundland. In reply to the hon. member's question I said that as I understood the question the culling of salted cod in Newfoundland was the responsibility of the provincial government, but that I would make a further reply later.
The situation, Mr. Speaker, is that cullers or graders of salted cod in Newfoundland are employees of the buyers of the product. Under the Newfoundland culling regulations originally promulgated by the commission of government, cullers are licensed. The system had been carried on by the federal Department of Fisheries following union, but the Department of Fisheries had no real supervision over their activities in the culling of salted cod.
During the past number of years the department has been concerned about the legality of its functions relative to the culling regulations. Accordingly, in consultation with the provincial government authorities it was established that the legal responsibility for enforcement of the Newfoundland culling regulations belonged to the province.
The federal department therefore is unable to assume further responsibility with respect to the Newfoundland culling regulations. The federal Department of Fisheries is, of course, continuing its responsibilities with respect to the inspection for export of Newfoundland salted cod, and has no intention of withdrawing from this legal responsibility. In the case of the first culling or grading, however, this is a matter between seller and buyer and comes, as I have said, within the authority of the province.
The provincial authorities asked the federal Department of Fisheries recently if we would
[Mr. Chevrier.)
administer the culling regulations on their behalf. After careful examination the provincial authorities were informed that to enforce the regulations properly and legally would require a large staff, and with the present organization of the federal Department of Fisheries in Newfoundland we could not undertake to administer the culling regulations on behalf of the province and at the same time carry out our responsibilities for the inspection and grading of salted cod for export.

Mr. Chairman, I should like at this time, before we proceed with consideration of the estimates of my department, to make a few remarks, first in relation to the department itself and to matters bearing on its services to industry, and second in relation to our mineral industry.
17, 1953	6197
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
By now all hon. members have had an opportunity to peruse the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters in connection with our estimates for the current fiscal year. Votes and Proceedings No. 87 of May 26 last contains the standing committee's summing up of the evidence they heard and their conclusions and recommendations.
It is not my intention to quote at length from this report but I should like to direct attention in particular to a paragraph which appears under its general section. This paragraph reads, and 1 quote:
"In almost all fields of national scientific endeavour, this department should have led and should lead the way . . . Both the people and those responsible for policy in Canada have been slow to realize the urgent need for expenditure and leadership in this field. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, your committee insists, must be recognized as a vitally important one, not one of inferior significance. The scientific function of the department cannot any longer be circumscribed by caution, hesitancy and lack of support. It is imperative that all branches of the department embark on an accelerated program of expansion, and planning for expansion; and that the provision of the needed money, staff and facilities be an immediate consideration of the government."
(Text):
May I also quote the last paragraph of the general section which reads:
Geography forces Canada to take a leading part in any northern matter, whether civil or military. This is an obligation which we cannot evade, but which we cannot fufil effectively without adequate research. For the effective development of the north a major expansion of research is essential. Without thorough and continuing research any development in the north is certain to be much more costly and may easily be misdirected.
I may state at this point that I am very pleased with the interest the members of the standing committee have shown in the activities of our department. It is abundantly clear from the tabled report from which I have just quoted that they put much time and earnest thought into the drafting of their conclusions. It is clear also that in its tasks in hand and possibly more so in those that lie ahead, my department has and will have an integral part to play in keeping Canada to the forefront in those important fields of science and engineering that bear particularly on resources development.
The standing committee places the greatest importance on the need for the activities in which the department is engaged. This need, it states in effect, is becoming so great and in some respects so urgent as to call for a major expansion of staff and facilities to cope with the requirements.
6198	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
In the evidence we gave to the standing committee we stated that over the next five years we shall need an additional staff of 1,440 including 305 seasonal employees to handle our assignments. We now have a staff of 3,785 including seasonals; thus the increase would bring the total up to 5,225 by the end of five years. By far the largest increase would be in our surveys and mapping branch, that for the Canadian hydrographic service alone being 490 continuing and 40 seasonal employees. The geological survey of Canada would be next with an estimated increase of 200 continuing and 175 seasonal employees. Our estimate of the additional staff that will be required is strongly endorsed by the standing committee; in fact they have recommended even larger increases in some cases, and most of these projections, I may state, seem more likely to be subject to upward rather than downward revision.
In a rapidly expanding economy such as we have in Canada the need for research is going to increase, and at an accelerated rate, according to present indications. As we look back over the 14 years that have passed since the war we marvel at the growth of the Canadian economy; yet if I were given to the use of trite expressions I would say, "We haven't seen anything yet". This, translated into more decorous phraseology, means that so far we have had little more than a glimpse of our growth potential.

Some of the major new projects we are undertaking this year will bear out what I have said concerning the role we have to play. Quite apart from their importance in other respects, they point up the urgency of much of our efforts-urgency in the sense that they are being undertaken to keep ahead of the requirements of industry or other urgent national demands and with the attention other countries are giving to scientific investigations.
One such project is the work we are undertaking on our polar continental shelf, which this year is simply exploratory to obtain an idea of the general character of the shelf, the equipment needed for such a project and the best type of transportation. Even though it is exploratory in character, it has already provided us with information that has caused us to revise our concepts of the area. The work to date appears to confirm the potentialities of the area as a source of petroleum, and further investigation will be aimed, in part, to determine whether these favourable conditions extend out over the shelf.

a geological reconnaissance of Banks and Victoria islands; the other in the Northwest Territories is a reconnaissance of a large area lying mainly west and south of Coppermine in a project we have named Operation Coppermine. In the Yukon project, we are commencing work this year in Operation Pelly, which is a reconnaissance of the southeastern portion of the territory.
I should explain here that in our geological work we have been giving top priority to reconnaissance projects since 1952, and we have already covered a total area of approximately half a million square miles, mainly in Northwest Territories and British Columbia. This is exclusive of the work in hand this year. The decision to give such projects top priority was mainly in an endeavour to complete the reconnaissance mapping of Canada in the foreseeable future and to keep abreast of the requirements of industry. A very important side aim of the work has been to develop low cost and efficient methods of mapping the areas concerned. By the use of helicopters and supporting fixed-wing aircraft, we have been able to cover as much ground in one season on these projects as would have required 20 to 25 years by the former methods and at a much lower cost.
In furtherance of our endeavours to reduce the cost and increase the efficiency, we made a test last year of the use of Piper Super Cub planes, equipped with wheels designed for landing on unprepared terrain. The tests proved so successful that the planes will be put to more extensive use this year on our geological reconnaissance of Banks and Victoria islands. The geologists will be able to make their observations from the planes and to land within easy walking distances of the places where samples or detailed observations are needed. We now have some reason to believe that, where this specially equipped plane can be used, the work can be done much more cheaply and efficiently than by use of the helicopter.
As the hon. members are probably aware, Mr. Chairman, my department has been given considerable attention to land-use mapping. The importance of such work in a rapidly growing country like Canada need not be stressed. The projects are being carried out in co-operation with the provinces concerned, our work this year being in Ontario, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia. In another project, our geographical branch is

The work this year is in the Mackenzie river delta and in the Great Whale river area on the east coast of Hudson bay.
In the field of metallurgical research, we have undertaken work recently on several interesting projects. One of these affords a typical example of our aid to industry.
It concerns the recent announcement by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited of its plans to proceed with the construction of an electric smelter for the production of pig iron. This is part of a long-range plan to set up an integrated steel industry in western Canada. The company has been accumulating large tonnages of iron oxide as a by-product from its roasting operations. For years it was felt that the impurities in the oxide would be harmful to steel made from it. Research in our laboratories showed that a satisfactory steel meeting all the requirements for structural steel could, in fact, be produced and the company was thus in a position to proceed with the project.
In quite a separate project, we have commenced basic research on nickel-alloy systems in order to increase our knowledge of these types of alloys which are essential to the efficient design of missile components and also of modern thermo power plants.

In reference to these and other research projects in the mines branch I should like to direct your attention to certain of the conclusions reached by the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, and I quote:
The research in this branch should be concentrated on the long range projects. The many and varied problems requiring immediate research should not continue to engage 90 per cent, as it does now, of the resources of this branch. This "first-aid" research should be assumed by private industry. This would free branch resources to deal with such important problems, requiring much research, as developing new alloys to meet the needs, for instance, of supersonic flight, extraction of heavy oils (tar sands) etc.
Speaking at the annual convention of the prospectors and developers association in Toronto on March 3 last Dr. van Steenburgh, our director general of scientific services, stated:
If a change of emphasis is made-

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
From applied to basic research, that is.
-it will mean that industry will need to either undertake more of its own applied research or to have it done by provincial research councils or by private research organizations. What is needed is a strengthening of the provincial research councils; that and the establishment of a few research institutes similar in nature to those organized in the United States.
Quoting further from his remarks, he stated;
-to do this would require sizeable funds to provide the initial buildings and equipment. In the United States, memorial bequests from wealthy patrons have been largely instrumental in solving the problem. In other countries it is being solved by co-operative arrangements between government and industry, a policy similar in some respects to that followed in establishing the provincial research councils.
Actually the choice seems to be between doing more and more basic and long term research at the government level and in the universities, or allowing Canada to lag in these fields of research to a dangerous degree. And here I should explain that I am not thinking simply in terms of research as it relates to the activities of my department, but of research in general.
We cannot, of course, allow our basic and long term research to lag to a dangerous degree. That, as I am sure hon. members will agree, could prove to be costly indeed, and not in terms of money alone. The only alternative appears to be for a much greater concentration of effort on basic and long term research at the government level. The question is, how can this be brought about?
Excellent research is being done by some of the large mining companies in Canada, but this is far from enough. To me the answer, in part at least, is for industry to give serious thought to the establishment of a research organization similar, for instance, to the Battelle institute in the United States. My suggestion is that industry provide the funds to establish such institutions, and perhaps also to finance the initial stages of their operations. The funds could be provided in different ways; possibly, for instance, in the form of contributions by individual companies or through such organizations as the Canadian metal mining association or the prospectors and developers association. If industry were to take such action it is possible that the federal government, with the consent of parliament, would be willing to either match the contributions from industry or at least contribute substantially to the establishment of such research institutions.
In so far as my own department is concerned, Mr. Chairman, their establishment, coupled with any enlargement of the facilities of the provincial research councils, would 

mean that we could devote a much greater proportion of our effort to basic and long term research, say 60 to 70 per cent of it or more. It would not mean, nor indeed would it be desirable, that we would discontinue research on problems of immediate interest to industry. Continuity of effort is an essential factor in work on these problems, and there could be no guarantee of such continuity in a research institute concerned not only with investigations bearing on mineral development but with the whole broad field of industrial research. Besides, much of our work is of benefit chiefly to small enterprises that are unable to finance or undertake their own research, and it is in the interests of the country as a whole that our facilities be used to aid them. It is important also that we continue our work on problems that are of concern to industry as a whole or to major segments of it. An example of this is the work of our mines branch on the economic processing of low grade ores. Usually the results of such work are of benefit to a number of companies rather than to a single company.
However, there are many time-consuming tests and investigations and numerous research problems that I am sure could be handled efficiently by organizations like the research institutes I have suggested should be established. We would then be free to devote a much greater proportion of our time to basic and long term research, and at the same time maintain the essential services to industry.
Turning now to our mineral industry, let us take a brief look at the status of the industry today in the Canadian economy and at the prospects it has in store. First, Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw your attention to the almost meteoric growth of our mineral industry during these post-war years. We are all aware that the industry has recorded remarkable expansion, but I venture to say that few of us realize that it has outstripped even the Canadian economy in rate of growth.
In its recent report the standing committee on mines, forests and waters drew attention to this fact. It pointed out that between 1947 and 1957 the index of physical volume of mineral production increased by 173 per cent while that of industry as a whole increased by 51 per cent.
We can gain an even better picture by using as our yardstick our gross national product at market prices. In 1946 it stood at $12 billion. By 1957 it has soared to $30 billion, an increase of 150 per cent.
At the same time the value of our mineral production quadrupled from $500 million to $2 billion, an increase of 300 per cent. And

even more astonishing is the fact, Mr. Chairman, that not only has the mineral industry outstripped the Canadian economy in rate of growth but, with the exception of construction, it has recorded a relative growth greater than that of any of Canada's other productive industries, including manufacturing, agriculture and lumbering.
Let me pause to illustrate this. Using 1946 as a base, we find that construction heads the list with a remarkable increase of 800 per cent. The mineral industry is second with a 320 per cent increase. Manufacturing, by far the greatest in volume, shows a rate of expansion of 177 per cent, and agriculture increased only 10 per cent.
Last year the mineral industry suffered its first setback since the close of world war II, but even at that the value of our mineral production at $2.1 billion was only 3 per cent below the all-time record of the preceding year. Our mineral industry is, as hon. members know, a major world supplier of metals and minerals and, as such, it felt the full impact of the weakening of world mineral markets and the twin evils of overproduction and price declines. Consequently the value of output of our principal base metals, copper, nickel, lead and zinc, as well as of iron ore, asbestos and crude petroleum, declined sharply.
Contributing to this setback were the discontinuation of the stockpiling program in the United States and the subsequent release of additional supplies of metals for industrial use; the imposition by that country of import quotas on lead and zinc, and of voluntary, followed by mandatory import restrictions on crude oil entering the mid-continent and western United States. These restrictions on oil, as you know, have since been lifted.
Over and above these difficulties, our mineral industry has faced increasing competition for world markets from Russia, particularly in asbestos, which is our chief industrial mineral. Partly as a result of this competition, our output of asbestos dropped off 10 per cent last year from the all-time high of over a million tons recorded in 1957.
You can readily see then, Mr. Chairman, that the over-all situation has not been conducive to the expenditure of large sums of money on exploration. Consequently in the past year or so there has been less activity in diamond drilling, less geophysical work, fewer claims staked, and less surface prospecting than in many a year. Lately, however, the picture has brightened. The general industrial pick-up, particularly in the United States, has already had a stimulating effect on the mining industry. Demand is strengthening, prices are improving and a general feeling of optimism pervades the industry.

A development of great significance to the industry and to the whole Canadian economy is the increasing trend toward the processing of ores and their products here in Canada This is seen in recent company announcements which include the proposed construction of a $20 million to $25 million nickel refinery in northern Manitoba and an iron smelter at Kimberley, British Columbia. The construction of the iron smelter is the first stage in a $20 million project planned to produce pig iron, steel ingots, and rolled steel products to serve the rapidly growing markets of our western provinces. Industry is also considering again the construction of a zinc refinery in eastern Canada. At present we are shipping the zinc concentrates that we produce in eastern Canada to the United States and to European countries for refining, but mostly to the central and northeastern states.
Looking ahead, the prospects for our mineral industry are good. The effect of the general industrial pick-up, which has already made itself felt on the industry, gives every indication of continuing. Unemployment has dropped. Construction activity is reaching new levels, and markets show signs of continuing to strengthen. Moreover, populations round the world continue to grow, steadily increasing the potential consumption of metals.

That we in Canada possess huge mineral resources is well known. On the more immediate mineral horizon, we have several good prospects. These are, for instance, the rich copper and zinc deposits which have come to light in the Mattagami-Frotet lake area of western Quebec; the largely undeveloped copper and gold Chibougamau area; the great reserves of iron ore in Quebec and in Ontario, especially, either under development or awaiting development; and the extensive lead-zinc deposits of northeastern New Brunswick and at Pine Point in Northwest Territories.
These are only a few. Consider, too, the great unexplored areas of our northland where a handful of discoveries has even now indicated the richness of resources there, awaiting exploration and development.
Truly, we in Canada, have the wealth and the opportunities. It is up to us to make the most of both.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys for this fiscal year were given a searching consideration at the standing committee of mines, forests and waters. Thirteen sittings of the committee were devoted to the study of this department's estimates. The directors of the various divisions of the department as well as the officials of the dominion coal board graciously answered the questions put to them by the members of the committee and they provided us with a lot of most useful information.
In our inquiries into all the items under this department we were able to appreciate that it is one of the best organized departments and that its staff is most competent. And at this time I would like to congratulate warmly all the directors, their assistants, their help, in short all those who belong to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys for the good work they are performing in the interest of the increasing development of our natural resources.
Since we have already devoted quite a long time to the consideration of these estimates in the standing committee of mines, forests and waters, and in view also of the fact that we have obtained in that committee all the information required, I assume that this committee does not intend to review each item in all its details. As far as I am concerned, I intend to be as brief as possible. My remarks will be along the line followed by the minister, that is to say I intend to speak firstly about the report which was tabled in the house on May 26 last, and then I would like to say a few words about the mining industry itself and point out, as did the minister, the problems and difficulties prevailing in this industry at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, while the report from the committee includes perhaps a few comments which might seem a little too strong, it contains many useful recommendations, and I feel that they will meet with the approval of all hon. members who sat on that committee. I was delighted to hear the minister say this morning that most of those recommendations would be carried out. Personally, I support most of them for I have always urged that something be done to step up the work of the department, and that it be voted all the funds it requires.
[Mr. Comtois.)

The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, with its present branches, was set up in the late fall of 1949 and put in operation some weeks later, on the 18th of January 1950, to be exact.
It has kept growing ever since. Each year it has taken on more staff and its budget allotment has increased considerably. In fact its net total estimated expenditure for the current fiscal year runs over $48 million.
Mr. Chairman, as a result, first, of mining activities in areas of known economic importance, especially since world war II, second, of the increased development rate of mineral resources throughout the country, especially during the period 1950 to 1958, and finally, of expanded prospecting and exploration in the northern regions of the provinces and in the territories, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has had so much to do that, while it provided for all the immediate needs of industry, it found it practically impossible to spearhead development in all fields and throughout the country.
If we want to step up the economic development of Canadian mineral ressources and to provide more efficient services to the mining industry, we shall clearly have to attach more and more importance to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
For that purpose, the report of the committee on mines, forests and waters includes several useful recommendations which, in my opinion, the government should not fail to act upon.
Thus, it is obvious that the department should take on more staff. From 1950 to 1959, the number of employees rose from 1725 to 3761, or rather 3785, as the minister indicated this morning; that represents an increase of 118 per cent in ten years, or an average annual increase of 11.8 per cent. Considering the amount of work to be done, and if we want the department at least to maintain the high standards of efficiency it has reached in the last decade, the committee's recommendation that the number of employees be increased from 3761 or 3885 to 5200, in the next five years, is certainly not unrealistic, for it represents an annual increase of only 7.6 per cent.
But increased staff also means increased expenditures and, there again, I repeat- if the government wishes to follow up that recommendation of the committee, and I believe it is bound to do so-it will have to agree to substantially higher appropriations.

I said a moment ago that the department's total estimated expenditures for this year were about $48 million. If we deduct the amounts earmarked for gold mining assistance under the act, and those provided under various items for the dominion coal board, total expenditures, which reached $11 million in 1950, have now reached $24.5 million, i.e. an increase of 123 per cent in the last ten years. This is an average yearly increase of 12.3 per cent. I imagine that if the committee's recommendations are followed up, the department's total estimates will reach at least $60 million in 1964.
Another important recommendation contained in the report of the committee deals with research activity. On that point again I was very happy to hear, or rather to notice this morning, that a good part of the minister's statement dealt with research undertaken by his department and told us of his intention to introduce a bill which might meet the approval of all concerned.
The mines branch of the department was established in 1907 under the Geology and Mines Act. It was meant as a research organization, and indeed, since its establishment, it has kept dealing especially with technical and scientific studies more particularly related to the development and the efficient and economic use of our considerable mineral resources. Those are the terms of reference of this branch, as defined in the report of the department for the year 1957.
According to the evidence given by high officials of the mines branch, it is essential that basic research take a more prominent place in Canada's mining industry. We were told that specialized research with regard to the treatment of complex ore were to be intensified, as such research would be of benefit to the country five or ten years hence. Lastly, we were told that the need or necessity of basic research was conditioned by several factors. There was reference, among other things, to the requirements of up-to-date development methods which make for increased production and better quality, and of the ever growing mining of low-grade, complex or refractory ore, etc.
It was as a result of this evidence that the committee recommended that the mines branch research should concentrate on long term development, that preliminary research be made by private industry and, finally, that private industry should take on a substantial share of the research now carried out by the mines branch.

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
In theory, Mr. Chairman, those recommendations may seem logical but, to my mind, fn practice they are not. It is true that some Canadian mining concerns may conduct research work to satisfy the greater part of their needs; the fact remains that most Canadian mining companies simply cannot undertake large scale research. In the first place, they lack the necessary funds and, more important, they lack and are unable to obtain a competent staff to conduct this work.
I think that the solution suggested this morning by the hon. minister should be seriously considered. I for my part, think his proposal is logical and I am sure that, if it were put into practice, the research division of his department and private companies, might be satisfied because the Canadian mining industry is aware of existing conditions, and intends to co-operate as far as possible with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. This has been clearly established in the committee by the branch director, Dr. Convey, when he was giving evidence, and I hope the committee will bear with me if I quote some of the information that Dr. Convey has been kind enough to give us and which can be found on page 296 of the English text, no. 12. This is what Dr. Convey said:
I will say this, that over the past 10 years Canadian industry has attempted to do some of their own research, but they seem to reach a stage in which they lack the personnel they are wanting, and the facilities, and that is when we come into co-operation with them. However, there are quite a few firms who are attempting to solve a lot of their own problems.
And Dr. Convey went on to say as follows:
Once we undertake a problem the company becomes more interested, and eventually what happens is that they go back home and do a lot of their own homework; and we co-ordinate this program in such a fashion that we literally demand that they become more than a sleeping participant.
Mr. Chairman, let the staff of this division be increased, let the division recruit the scientists and technicians it may require, and here I am referring to the mines division of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, let it get the necessary equipment, let it have the necessary sampling plants and laboratories. That is basic, and I am all for it.
However it is definitely necessary that this division keep co-operating with industry and help industry solve the many and various
6204	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys problems which call for immediate research. Of course, Mr. Chairman, we must encourage private industry by every means possible to undertake a much greater share of preliminary research here in Canada.
Personally, I would be very happy if the department, in co-operation with mining companies, were to set up a laboratory such as the one operated in the United States, by the Battelle research institution, which the minister has mentioned. In my view, this would be a great step forward. However, it is imperative that in the meantime, the mines branch should go on supplying all the data that most of our mining companies cannot get for themselves. If we want our industry to keep expanding, it is essential that the department give continued help to mining companies.
At this point, I should like to put on the record the remarks, made by Dr. Convey at a meeting of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, about research and the possibility of setting the pace. Here is what Dr. Convey said, as recorded on page 298 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, and I quote:
Through our efforts, we hope to stimulate our own industry to look after themselves, and our hope is that we can look to the day when we in the government laboratories can attend to those long-term research propositions which will be of benefit to the whole industry, and not to a particular part of industry.
I fully agree with these remarks of Dr. Convey. A little farther down, he added:
I have no doubt in my mind that if we can set the pace, industry will follow along.
Mr. Chairman, about this matter of giving leadership, I strongly urge the minister to carry out the recommendation put forward by the mines branch to the effect that an annual grant be established under his department, to encourage some bright university graduates-and here I am quoting the exact words used by Dr. Convey in the committee on mines, forests and waters:
-in order to try and encourage, at least in one field, some bright university graduates to enter the field of mining research.
Mr. Chairman, summing up my remarks concerning the report that was published following the discussions in the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, may I point out that I am in full agreement with those who hope the department will play a

leading role in the development of our natural resources. If the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is to retain the prestige it has acquired since it came into being, the government will of course have to give serious consideration to the provision of necessary funds, as well as of staff and facilities.
While the mining industry has developed tremendously since world war II-and I do not propose to go over the history of the development of that industry since then, because that I am sure that the minister has given a true and satisfactory summary this morning-mining is now facing certain difficulties. I do not want to magnify those difficulties, as I don't want to be pessimistic. I am rather optimistic as far as that industry is concerned. However, mining naturally feels the effects of the present slowdown in all branches of the Canadian economy. Metal prices have deteriorated, there has been overproduction, our friends to the south have clamped export restrictions on us, the industry is feeling the effects of inflation, and the rate of the exchange of the Canadian dollar is much too high, I believe.
In 1958 for the first time in many years, the total value of mineral production in Canada has declined. By the end of 1957, and at the beginning of 1958, prices of certain metals like copper, zinc and lead took such a drop that we wondered for a time, and rightly so, whether many mines would not be forced to close down. In fact, there has been a rather marked slow-down in development, prospecting and exploration.
The average price of copper in 1958 was 25.7 cents a pound, 13 per cent less than in 1957. Quite recently-and we are quite happy about it-the average price reached 31.5 cents a pound, but unfortunately, those last few weeks, it has dropped again to about 30 cents a pound. I hope we can look forward to the time when it will be possible to get a firm price for that metal, as well as for the others.
Prices of lead and zinc are low, and it is quite possible that they will stay low for quite a while yet.
Another very important problem with which the industry is now faced-the minister dealt with the matter a few moments ago- is that of American stockpiling of strategic metals. The possible liquidation even of a small part of those stocks, is a continuing

threat to the industry. Let us hope that the United States government will transfer those reserves to stockpiles already considered as national reserves, and will give us the assurance that those reserves will not be marketed, except in case of extreme urgency.
It is probably the marketing of certain quantities, however small, of those stocks of strategic metals, which is causing fluctuations on the copper market. The price of copper is up one day and down the next. I hope that this matter will be settled once and for all, for the benefit of the industry.
The mining industry, in common with our whole economy, feels the continued inflationary pressures, which are a serious danger to them. Competition for world markets is keener than it ever was. As I mentioned on a previous occasion several ore-producing countries where wages and production costs are often merely a fraction of those in Canada, are developing their own resources at a great pace.
Again, Mr. Chairman-and it would be well to consider this-we must always remember that the Canadian mining industry depends on our export trade, and that our mineral resources are an asset only to the extent that they are developed, produced and marketed. Otherwise, they are only worthless rock. This self-evident truth should not be ignored.
Another problem which must never be overlooked is that of uranium. I do not intend to dwell on this subject, since it was dealt with yesterday, and I believe the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) spelled out what has to be done in that regard. I only hope the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) will see to it that the Leader of the Opposition's recommendations made in the house yesterday will be followed up.
If the mining industry is now labouring under certain difficulties, as the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated, I believe future possibilities are rather encouraging.
In the last decade-and that is very interesting-world consumption of metals has increased considerably. In that same period, world consumption of copper, for instance, has increased by a million tons, or 35 per cent. As the standard of living rises in under-developed countries, it will certainly promote increased use of base metals.
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
Therefore, Canada is bound to get a growing share of the expanding world demand for metals, and Canadian producers can look with confidence to the long term market prospects.
Canadian mining concerns hope and expect to remain the main suppliers of metals of all kinds on the United States market, for generations to come, and in ever increasing volumes.
However, in the meantime, we have some responsibilities. Everything should be done to keep the industry in top condition. Steps should be taken to ensure the highest possible level of employment in the mines, and we must see that Canadian producers are not forced to beneficiate their ore, and thus reduce the life of their mines. This is a most important point. If companies are forced to mine higher grade ores, it could shorten the life of the mines.
We must encourage prospecting and exploration by all possible means. We have the technical know-how and I cannot see why our country could not be at the forefront in that field. It is a branch of our economy which must remain sound and strong.
Mr. Chairman, I have taken quite an interest in the comments that the minister made this morning. His statement, while somewhat long, was genuinely interesting and contained several very practical ideas. Personally, I am interested in mining industry, I want it to keep on growing and, with the help of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, I am sure that we will reach that goal.

But I should like to point out that unlike the work done on forestry later, in which the concentration was upon outside witnesses rather than anything else to bring us information, the information we had on the main estimates of

The report presented represents a stunning indictment of government policy and lack of ministerial leadership in the last number of years. I do not know that we can absolve even the present minister. I wish to read what is perhaps the most critical section of the committee report, which refers to the mines branch:
83. The information elicited on the mines branch was depressing. The branch does not have the funds for the staff it needs to carry out the work it should do and wants to do.
About ten points are listed concerning the mines branch, which indicate the situation has not been good. There is no use labouring the point. We should watch this department perhaps more closely than any other department of government in the next year or two.
Parliamentary committees have now reviewed most departments of government, and no department to my knowledge was raked over the coals to the extent this department was in terms of not fulfilling the functions it was designed to fulfil. This is a more critical report even than that tabled yesterday on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in some respects, and I hope the minister and his deputy appreciate the seriousness of the criticisms contained therein. You cannot find much flattering in the report about the work the department has done. As I said, the information that led to the criticism came from the officials themselves, which is a great mark in their favour. It is an indication that they know what they would like to do and where they would like to go. It seemed to me to suggest a genuine lack of ministerial leadership.
In the little game that is played in this chamber it is customary for questions of this kind to be tossed back and forth between the government and the opposition, each disclaiming responsibility. I helped prepare the report, and it is clear that most of the responsibility rests with the previous government for letting this department fall behind in the obligations it should have been pursuing.
One recommendation not mentioned by the previous speaker refers to the work of the geographical branch in paragraph 93, referring to land use. A big conservation conference is planned for 1960. If we are going


to go in for more and better forestry and land use this branch of the department is going to have to make provision for greater and more detailed surveys.
I am always pleased when I can compliment someone in Ontario, and we have in this province a group very much interested in land use. Last year they held a conference in the Niagara peninsula and went into the whole question of cost benefit studies and land use in this region, where some of the finest agricultural soil in the country is going out of crop production because of industrial expansion. Soil experts, geographers, foresters, engineers and people interested in the natural topography of Canada in its many facets agree that we have to come to grips with this problem. We look forward to this forthcoming conference and hope the department and especially the geographical branch will plan on making a vital contribution to its success. Perhaps later the minister will give us an indication of the contribution that will be made.
I wish now to refer to gold mining assistance. Following remarks I made on this subject last year the Northern Miner, a puff sheet well known in the mining trade, which exploits stocks and gives the latest gossip in the trade, severely took me to task for calling into question the integrity of mining companies. They stated that I was completely wrong in my understanding of the situation with respect to gold mining assistance. The paper is entitled to its views, and I mention it only because I propose to bring up the same points now.
Under section 6	(a) of the Emergency
Gold Mining Assistance Act inspectors of the department have the right to go and inspect mine workings. Last February 3 the minister filed an answer to questions of mine as reported at page 666 of Hansard of that date. The questions were as follows:
1.	How many times and in what years before 1958 did inspection engineers of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys use the powers given under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act (R.S. 1952; c. 95) section 6, subsection (a) "to enter upon and examine the mine from which the gold in respect of which the payment is to be made is produced" in so far as the following mines are concerned-
A list then appeared of Ontario mines in receipt of assistance. I continue:
2.	On any of such kind of inspections were drawings and plans of the workings checked with the actual workings?
3.	If so, on what occasions?

The answers read as follows:
1.	An inspection engineer from the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys carried out an annual inspection, under the provisions of section 6 of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, of the mines listed, for each of the years from 1948 to 1957 inclusive. In general, the inspections did not include an examination of the underground workings.
2.	No.
3.	Not applicable.
We have been sitting in the broadcasting committee where the Conservative members in particular have expressed themselves as terribly keen on getting at the roots of all these subsidies. We have to make sure the C.B.C. is not wasting our money; we are really going to go into the thing thoroughly. In this instance we are giving millions of dollars to private corporations under federal legislation, and the inspectors of this department do not even bother to examine the underground workings of the mines. They go into the offices, that is all.
This is not a case of my raising questions about the integrity of corporations. If we believe that the spending of public money should be checked to see that we get value for it, then it is up to those inspectors to do something more than just to walk into the mine office. I also understand from the information I received from the department that these inspectors are on the property for maybe half a day; they just visit around.
How in the name of all that is sane can you have any kind of check of millions spent in that way if you just have a fellow drop in for a day? Surely if the Conservative members of this house are going to be suspicious at all times of government subsidies that are going out to crown corporations, then I think they have, and I think the minister needs, to adopt a bit of suspicion toward companies that are receiving this money. It seems to me this is the kind of consistency we should have.
I should like to know from the minister why these inspectors do not do much more checking of those companies. We gave them examples last year of a couple of mines that we were suspicious of in one particular field. The miners with whom I happen to have a fair amount of contact tell me that stopes are cemented up, that various rich veins are just passed by while the company goes on to mine something of a lower grade. I know in this whole question of mining different grades there is a great deal of leeway left open to
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys the mine officials. It is a complicated procedure. But I would feel much better about these millions being poured into these gold mines if we knew the inspectors were going to run a real check on them. A man who spends half a day on a property and does not even go underground is not an inspector; he is just a travelling salesman handing out money. I suggest to the minister that there should be a more thorough inspection.
There is another aspect of the emergency gold mining assistance that bothers me and perhaps some other members of the house, and that is the trend in the gold mining industry to consolidate and move toward monopoly. For example there is one syndicate, the Little Long Lac syndicate, that in the last couple of years has been gobbling up a whole group of mines. Among the mines, as an example, was MacLeod-Coekshutt. A number of people in my particular region were small share holders in that mine, which was a fairly sound one, a low-cost producer. It had no tremendous future, but it was paying regular dividends, and the actual share value of the stock was not particularly high.
Here were people-and I can give some other instances-who had very low incomes, people who were pensioned off, who were counting on these dividends. What has happened with this monopoly trend type of thing? We know this is financed by big men in the market who are able to play the thing, but for the little person it is pretty tough. They took over without having to go to the trouble of purchasing all the shares; they took over many of these smaller companies, and consolidated the operations. I suppose they may be making them more efficient; they certainly have more money to provide for further exploration and maybe to develop this particular mine's properties. But what has happened in these particular cases is that the dividends almost always stop.
In so far as Little Long Lac is concerned, that is so. The smaller shareholder has no protection; he, of course, has no real voice in the shareholders' meetings. This is one of the laughs about the democracy of a company set-up; the small shareholder is just a joke. He can only say this. He had shares in this mine which were bringing him some dividends. All of a sudden the mine is taken over by a bigger corporation and the dividends stop, but the emergency gold mining assistance goes right on.
In the MacLeod-Cockshutt case, as I remember it, the dividend that was paid for a number of years almost equalled what that mine was getting from the government. Well, the dividend stops but the emergency gold mining assistance goes right along. How can you blame the small stockholder, the
6208	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys small investor, for feeling that in effect in these circumstances the government is subsidizing with emergency gold mining assistance a group that is extending its tentacles to cover a great deal of the mining world.
I am neither an expert nor a critic of the building up of these large corporations that control a number of mines. I tend to distrust them, though I know there are a number of socialist economists who say it is nothing more than a natural trend that is going to lead to a new corporate structure that is largely going to be in government hands. But without getting into the inevitability of those developments, here is a case where a government subsidy is going to mines and those mines are in this position. It looks as though in the years ahead they will not be paying any dividends, but that the increment value will come to the people who own large blocks of stock in the holding group as a whole.
Last year my hon. friend from Timiskam-ing raised a point. He wanted to make a change in the act which would force the mines to give a certain percentage of the emergency gold mining assistance to their employees. I still think there is something valid in that point, but I would like to ask the minister a question on this other point. Does he consider it fair, or does he think he can do anything about this situation, where several hundred thousands of dollars will go to a mine that should be a going operation with that assistance, and nothing ever gets to the shareholders? I think it is a most questionable operation. If those mines are kept going only in terms of emergency gold mining assistance I think we need to re-examine the monopoly conditions that are developing in that gold mining industry.
I know the minister will probably say that this is something for the Minister of Justice and the combines investigation branch, but I suggest to him that it is also something for him, because it certainly is an irony that millions of dollars of the government's money are spent in keeping those gold mines going. The communities are all behind it. This is one of the ironies. You have the community people, the unions, the service clubs and everybody else out beating the drum for the mining companies because they want to keep the mines going, they want to keep them alive; but what is actually happening to the money in some of these cases, and especially in the Little Long Lac case?
That, Mr. Chairman, covers what I wanted to say on emergency gold mining assistance, the question of inspection and the question of the failure of some of these companies to


carry on the practices of the past. That is the real point of the monopoly of the big holding company structure. I hope that next year when the minister appears with his estimates we will be able to say, he has put on an excellent show in carrying out the recommendations that were made by the committee. I certainly hope that if the committee sits again the officials of the department will display the same candour and honesty they displayed this year.
I do not mean to say there was anything odd about their candour and honesty, but I certainly feel that, much more than any other government officials I have ever heard giving evidence, they tried to be as frank and as blunt as possible, and for that they are surely to be commended. I hope the minister will remember that the past policy of the department can be much criticized for creating a despondent state throughout the department, and that he will make sure that such criticisms will never need to be made again, at least in his time in this particular department.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a few words. I do not want to take up too much of the committee's time, but before the first vote of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is carried, I would like to make a few remarks. I also support the remarks of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) with regard to departmental senior officials who, unquestionably, are very conscientious, deeply interested in mining and particularly anxious to assist that industry and prospectors of new mineral deposits throughout Canada.
I would also like to tell the minister how much we appreciated his visit, in our district last autumn, when he came to look at the mines in western Quebec, to gather first-hand information on the conditions and future requirements of the mines. I therefore take this opportunity to tell him that we all have pleasant memories of his visit and I hope that he too will remember with pleasure the proverbial hospitality of people in western Quebec.
And now, I should like to offer to the minister a suggestion with regard to geological surveys in my area, more particularly in the riding of Chapleau, which I have the honour to represent in this house.
I know, for instance, that a good many aeromagnetic surveys have been carried out through his department in western Quebec
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys for the past few years, and they are very important, indeed. They supply very useful information not only to mining companies but to prospectors and to anyone interested in mining development, either in western Quebec-an area of particular interest to me personally-or anywhere else in this country where such surveys are taking place.
The minister told us this morning that similar surveys are being carried out in some districts of northern Ontario, near the Manitoba boundary, and in various other places in this country. However, in addition to those aeromagnetic surveys, I think it would be well to undertake other and more detailed geological surveys in various areas and, more particularly in the district of lakes Kitchigama, Mattagami, Waswanipi, Bachelor and Opawica, to mention a few names that occur to me. Those lakes are located along what is called a mineralized zone, a mining zone, in the central area of the constituency of Chapleau, about midway between the present settlements along the railway line, and James bay, farther north. No geological survey has been made along that mineralized zone for at least 20 years.
As I said earlier, certain aeromagnetic surveys were made there, but no detailed geological survey. In my opinion, those geological surveys would be quite useful, not only to prospectors, but to mining companies. I believe very useful data could be got from the mining companies now operating in that area. Some of them have gone in for diamond-drilling on a rather large scale, especially in the last couple of years. Those borings are uncovering geological data which would indeed be worth compiling for use in drawing more detailed maps for prospectors and mining companies. To my knowledge, the last detailed geological maps of that region which have been published are known as the maps of Mattagami and eastern and western Chibougamau region. More detailed maps of that region have not been made for more than 20 years.
The provincial department of mines has made a few, but I believe the federal government would do well to consider the matter, so as to promote development of Canada's mining resources. The government should also undertake to have more detailed geological maps published, not only of the regions I just referred to, but also of new mining regions where necessary.

Before lunch the hon. member for Port Arthur again raised this problem of emergency gold mining assistance and some of the charges and countercharges that have been made in regard to this matter over the past number of years. It might have been brought to the attention of the committee that last year when this question of emergency gold mining assistance was raised, several of us who represent mining areas had unkind things to say about some of the activities of some of the mines. I am quite satisfied with some of the reports that appeared at that time, one of which was carried in the Northern Miner, which is a mine publication, and we know what to expect from such publications.
This newspaper went on to say that I have had some experience in mines and I should not be allowed to make these statements, that these statements should not go unchallenged. They said I should not take advantage of the fact I am a member of parliament to make these charges. Well, Mr. Chairman, I agree with what was said. I agree with what the Northern Miner said, that I should not make these charges without being able to do something about them. I therefore telephoned at my own expense to Timmins, where I worked before, and communicated with several people in the mining industry with whom I had worked and whose word I could accept. I asked them to make inquiries and give me the numbers and levels of the stopes of two of the major mines in this area that were closed off and used only on rare occasions to supplement the grade of ore from that mine. I received a telegram containing this information which I communicated to the department. I was informed at that time that the department did not have any inspectors who had checked the stopes; they did not know whether they were operating or not operating, so they were not in a position to check this information.

Personally I do not intend to make a fuss about it this year. Unfortunately we are faced with a situation where we are working against a deadline. Everybody is very anxious to go home, so I would not want to go into this matter at great length at this time. I am convinced also that the department has not done anything about it as yet, and I am only referring to this matter again so the department will have a look at this particular problem. Then next year, when we have these estimates before us, I should like to know exactly what stopes are being mined in the various mines; what is the condition of the reserves; where the reserves are, and we would like to have not only the blueprints of those particular stopes but we would like to have an inspector go into the mine on regular occasions and inspect the workings to see if, in fact, these operations are being conducted. Then if I give information to the minister that number such and such a stope in such and such a level is not being operated because of the high grade ore in that stope, the minister will be in a position to send an inspector there immediately to check on the situation and take action under the powers the minister is given by the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
I believe that in so far as every department is concerned, the Canadian National Railways, T.C.A., C.B.C. and all the other departments this government controls, we must-I agree with the Conservative members who have been crying very loudly- have some check on these organizations that come under the control of parliament. I believe also that hon. members would support me in saying that we must have some control over these large mining companies that have been using unsatisfactory methods in operating their mines.
At the time I made these complaints the department told me that this was good housekeeping practice. It may be from the mine's point of view very good housekeeping practice. I can see the reason for it. As was pointed out to me not long ago, there are no great fluctuations in most of these mines.
I think any person who has knowledge of mining operations knows that this does not happen; it is a condition that is created. Normally you would find probably three really good veins, and if at the same time you were mining a low grade vein your millheads might go away up. In most of the mines this does not happen. It does not happen because they sweeten up the low grade ore with high grade ore.
I suggest this may be very good housekeeping practice but, Mr. Chairman, this was not the purpose in raising the matter.

We made charges and I repeat them, that some of these mines have been low grading certain stopes, and this is contrary to the effective operation and the avowed purpose of emergency gold mining assistance.
I have the largest gold mine in America in my riding and, incidentally, it gets no assistance whatever from the government. On behalf of those people who depend on mines that are getting emergency gold mining assistance, we thank the minister for having increased the subsidy to the mines. Obviously this assistance must be reflected in the wages that are paid and in the conditions that exist in these communities, because these communities are entirely dependent upon this industry for their support.
We have asked in the past, at least some of us in this group-this may not come within the purview of the minister-that consideration be given to using some emergency gold mining assistance to help those areas that are completely dependent on gold mines in establishing secondary industries. No matter how long we continue to pay this form of subsidy to these gold mines, there will come a day when they will be completely mined out.
While it is true, from Canada's point of view, that new mining fields will be found and new mines opened up, the people in the existing gold mining communities depend on this government, now through emergency gold mining assistance and in future through some other form of assistance, to help them transfer their economy from total dependence on gold mining to secondary industry. Some of these communities have existed for 30 or 40 years, and it seems to me the time has now come when we should be looking very carefully at what is going to happen in the future.
This is all the more important when we remember that this act still has the word "emergency" in its title. It is not considered to be a permanent measure. We used to pass it every year until we gave it these additional three years of life. We are going to be faced again, the day it expires, with having to do something in that field. I suggest that the minister give very serious consideration to devising some other use for the amount of money the government is paying so we may be able, through this assistance, to eliminate the need for emergency gold mining assistance. In my opinion this can only be accomplished if we can introduce secondary industries into those areas.
Perhaps this point does not come within the jurisdiction of the minister, but if the minister could convince his colleagues that we should
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys have an increase in the price of gold I think a great deal of argument could be put forward for this proposition. It has not been, in the past, my practice to argue for an increase in the price of gold, for one or two very good reasons, the first being that Canada has supported the international monetary fund which has supported the sale of gold at a fixed price. I am aware also of the fact that the United States is one of the largest consumers of gold because, although we are not on the gold standard, gold is used to back our currency, its use in currency is endorsed by congress, and the amount of gold is set by the constitution.
Despite all these things, it also has a relationship to the price of real estate and the value of commodities. As inflation continues to increase, the arguments grow, and they are dramatized for an increase in the price of gold and a return to solid the backing of our currency by gold. This is a matter to which the minister can give consideration. I think he can urge the Minister of Finance to again put forward the argument in the international monetary fund and in our negotiations with the United States, pushing and working toward a higher price for gold.
This, I should like to point out, will not only solve the problem of emergency gold mining assistance, but it will solve the problem of expanding our production of gold very rapidly. I think there are few members here who have not at one time or another received a piece of information from one or more mining companies or mining promoters that has pointed out that if certain conditions are met-and one of them in an increase in the price of gold-the property they are offerring to you at 2 or 3 cents a share will be worth $15 or $20. I think it is quite obvious to everyone that an increase in the price of gold will stimulate a vast increase in our production of gold and in the search for that extremely valuable commodity.
There is another problem to which I should like to refer. It has been raised in Blind River. It covers the matter of another type of subsidy. I refer to the subsidy paid under the uranium clause to the mines in that area. I think the minister should give us some information on just how this subsidy from the government to the various mines is worked out. In negotiations to obtain more money for workers in a particular mine we are often told that if the wage factor goes up, then of course the amount of money the company will receive is going to be that much less. But we are told in this particular case in Elliot Lake, in the uranium industry, that the amount of money is tied to dominion

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys bureau of statistics figures and has no relationship to the wages that are paid in that particular industry. This publication goes on to say:
Here's how it is done. The yearly average hourly wage figure for Canadian mining other than gold is multiplied by $1.25 and then divided by $1,858 (both of these latter figures are fixed in the uranium contracts). The difference between the resulting figure and $1.25 (23 cents in 1958) is then paid to each uranium mining company on every pound of uranium oxide shipped to Eldorado. Depending on changes in the Canada-wide survey of average hourly earnings, the figure for 1959 and succeeding years may be greater than 23 cents per pound.
Here according to our calculations is what some of the local mines creamed off in 1958 as a result of the "joker" clause:
Algom	 $1,074,330.00
Denison	 975,145.03
Northspan	 968,332.89
Milliken	 264,040.00
Stanleigh	 256,092.35
This contract that has been worked out for the uranium has been a very hush-hush type of agreement as far as publication is concerned. I should like to ask the minister whether he has any information he would like to give on this matter, and how this type of clause was arrived at. This has been subsidized by the taxpayers, and is not in anything like as understandable form as the emergency gold mining assistance. I would suggest that if this type of subsidy is going to be employed, we should have an act that will cover it in the same way as is done under emergency gold mining assistance, and which will be administered by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys.
In closing I should just like to suggest to the minister that some consideration again be given to this matter of inspectors in the mines. I think the federal department could do a great deal of good if they were to give consideration to some of the conditions that have resulted from the present system.
While this matter is not at the present time under the minister's department, I suggest that more consideration should be given through his research department to some of the diseases and some of the working hazards of mining. I am thinking of the fact that in many of the provinces we have different mining regulations governing such matters as silicosis, bursitis, pneumococcus and some of the dermatitis problems that are raised by these various types of ore, and also this problem of uranium mining and some of the hazards that go with it. While, as I say, it has not been a problem with which the federal department of mines has been concerned, I think it is becoming increasingly necessary for them to give consideration to these matters.
[Mr. Peters.)
I should like to refer only to this particular case that I think has been repeated hundreds and hundreds of times across the country. I know it is true in my own area and I am certain it is true in the riding of the hon. member for Timmins, as well as in others. I refer to silicosis and how it has been treated in various provinces. I would recommend to all hon. members that they read and article that appeared in Liberty in November, 1958 entitled "My Husband Had to Die to Get Workmen's Compensation".
I think this article highlights one of the problems. This man and his wife for eight years conducted a battle with the compensation board in British Columbia. Then the wife sat on the doorsteps of the parliament buildings for some weeks and finally brought this matter to the attenton of many of the citizens of that province. When an autopsy was performed it was established that this man had silicosis and she was awarded a pension.
I agree that at the present time this is not a federal matter, but as technocracy advances and as the various forms of technical advance take place, I think we should be more and more willing to bring equality to workers, no matter in what province they live, where it is possible to do so through the federal department. I suggest that the minister give consideration to some of these diseases which are not even recognized by some of the provincial compensation boards. I am not suggesting that we interfere with the rights that have been given to the provinces, but there are fields of research that could be undertaken and some standardization of this research that I am sure would be beneficial to all workers throughout the country.

However, he referred in particular to the price of copper, saying that the price in 1958 was 25 cents, that in 1959 it went up to 31 i cents, but that it is now 30 cents.
When, last year, I visited the area represented by the hon. member for Villeneuve, I was told by company officials that if the price remained at 30 cents a pound everybody would be happy. I do think that if it remains at that level and if the prospects hold, there will be no decline in mining operations.
