And now I think I should say a few words about what was said by the hon. member for Port Arthur. He mentioned that there was a lot of criticism in the report of the committee on mines, forests and waters. Well, the recommendations made by that committee will surely help me to convince the government that more should be done in research and improvements in our department. Mr. Chairman, when I was appointed to be in charge of the department, things were as they were, and I must say that we are moving as fast as we can in that regard.
Another point was raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur, who has quite properly shown interest in the proper administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I wish to assure him that my department and the Department of Finance are vigilant in ensuring that moneys are paid only after a thorough investigation of the cost of operation of every gold mining company which is eligible for assistance.
In answer to a question by the hon. member from Port Arthur, it was stated that the drawings and plans of the underground workings of every gold mine were not checked with the actual workings. I should like to point out that a limited underground visit would produce only superficial checks on the completeness of the mine plans. Such an inspection would be of no benefit unless a check survey of the underground workings were made and the grades and quantities of ore mined from the various working places
17. 1959	6213
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys were substantiated. Such a procedure would duplicate the work of the engineering staff at each mine, and would require a duplication of their number as inspectors. It is for this reason that direct examination of underground workings is undertaken only where unusual conditions exist. Far more effective checks on the operation and mining practices followed by a mine are obtained by the examination and correlation of mine plans from the engineering department, and the costs applicable to the various categories of mining operations from the accounting department.
It is in the interest of a gold mine operator to include in the costs which he submits for approval all the mining costs which have been incurred during the period. Unless he does so the amount of assistance he receives will be reduced. If a section of the underground workings is included in the costs but not shown on the plans, our usual examination of the plans of the work done and the costs attributable thereto would show at some point an abnormal and unsupported increase, thus calling for a further investigation of the matter. The table the minister was good enough to permit me to have reproduced in the record illustrates over a wide range of costs the effect on profit where assistance is paid and where assistance plus 25 per cent is paid. As costs increase beyond $25.20 an ounce the effect of assistance is to slow down
the declining profit rate rather than to provide for its maintenance. For instance, with assistance the break-even point on costs is extended from $35 to $45 an ounce.
The table also shows that the greatest profit is won with low costs and that, as the cost of producing an ounce of gold increases,


profits drop off very sharply. For instance, a profit of $20 an ounce can be made with a cost of $15 an ounce, but this drops to $10 with costs of $25, to $8.50 with costs of $26.50 and to $6.94 with costs of $30, to $4.72 with costs of $35, to $2.50 with costs of $40 and to zero with costs of over $45.
The veins in an average gold mine have a wide range in grade from probably less than one-twentieth of an ounce to several ounces to the ton of ore. Usually the number of tons of high grade ore is quite limited, and as the grade decreases the number of tons increases. A picture of it could appropriately be shown in the form of a pyramid with a small peak of high grade ore and a large base of low grade ore.
Mines like to have a three year supply of ore available at all times for the mill, and one of the tasks of management is to determine that mixture of the various grades from which a maximum profit can be won. Only by earning a maximum profit is the best use made of the resource itself and of the labour and capital provided for its development and production.
I should now like to cite an example. Assume we have an oreshoot ten feet wide by 480 feet long. This would yield 400 tons per vertical foot. Assume the recoverable grade to be 0.20 ounces or $7 with gold at $35. Assume cost per ton at $6. The cost per ounce would be $30. The cost aid would work out to $1.94 per ounce or 39 cents per ton. It would be bad practice to try low grading, because you have to make a profit. You
17. 1959	6215
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys have to mine the ore you have. It is good practice to try to keep an average grade. This was done by the responsible management of many gold mines in an effort to lengthen the life of the mines. We have many examples where companies tried to mine only high grade. The hon. member for Port Arthur complained about some of these.
Some mines do this in order to pay high dividends to their shareholders. One mine in Quebec paid 15 per cent on the money invested in the mine, but the mine had only a short life. Management was not wise enough to establish an average grade and a fair profit. The mine is not now in existence. It was giving employment to 300 or 400 men but now it is closed, though it could have been in operation for another 25 or 30 years. This is an example of the result of high grading. If you do low grading you achieve the same result, because if you do not make a profit on a mine it has to be closed down.
Another question was raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur regarding the amalgamation of some companies. He may have good reason to complain in the case of MacLeod-Cockshutt; I do not know. In Malartic one company acquired three mines previously under separate management, one of which was going to be closed down with salvage operations about to begin. The previous management was discouraged. I will not say there was bad management, but it appears that they did not have the courage to undertake additional exploration in order to find more ore in the mine.
These mines were taken over by a certain company through shares bought at a cost higher than the market cost. They acquired control of the mines and because of good management found an ore body which prolonged the life of the mine for another 20 to 25 years.
When I talk about this question and about the operation of Little Long Lac, I am not talking in favour of any person or group of persons owning Little Long Lac; I am talking for the electors of my constituency, for the people of my own home town who know the situation. Today that mine would be closed if it had not been taken over by a group of people who are interested in mining. They found an ore body, and the life of that mine has been extended for another 20 or 25 years.
I have another example. Little Long Lac took over another mine, Malartic Goldfields Limited. It was claimed that there was no more ore in this mine and they were to enter into a salvage operation. Well, they did not find any ore there; maybe they found some, perhaps 200,000 or 300,000 tons, which

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys is lengthening the life of the mine for maybe a year or two. But what else did they do? They acquired two small prospects near that mine. They bought those prospects, and again they bought the stock at a higher price than they would have paid on the market. They bought those two prospects; they did the exploration work. They are doing the development work in such a way that Malartic Goldfields, which employs 600 men, instead of closing in one or two years from now, will be able to operate for another 15 or 20 years.
This is the result of the coming of Little Long Lac to my home town of Malartic. The people of Malartic are very happy today because people with some vision came there and did something to prolong the life of those mines. That is the situation. Maybe it is different somewhere else, I do not know; but I feel that if a group of people get together and are ready to take a chance and buy a gold mine or a copper mine-you do not buy those by just bidding a certain price; you have to buy control. You have to buy shares. You have to buy them on the market, or you have to buy them from a group of people who have those shares. What did Little Long Lac do? They went to the people who had control of the company and said, "We will pay you 15 cents or 20 cents more a share than the price of those shares on the stock market, because we are interested".
That is the situation, and that is the story of Little Long Lac in my home town of Malartic. I did not want to allow this matter to go unchallenged because the life of my constituency, which depends on gold mining and base metal mining, was at stake, and we want this industry to be as healthy as possible.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

The hon. member who has just spoken has given one side of the story, and there are two. He presented a large number of figures, but in those figures there were certain weaknesses. His description of mining conditions in his home town sounded very much like conditions in my own home town, where there is much more mining done elsewhere than in the mine. The hon. member spoke as if he was doing actual work in the mining of ore, and I expected to see it piled over in the corner some place.
With respect to these charges of low grading and high grading, there are cases which have come to my knowledge. I have talked with people who know exactly where those stopes are or they would not make the charges. The men who work in the mines do not do this because the grade of ore fluctuates; they do it to obtain a particular level, which is quite a low level. There is something to be said for maintaining ore at a particular level


that the hon. member did not mention, and that is that the mills are designed to function with a certain millhead and a certain rate of recovery. If you dump in a large quantity of high grade ore or if you dilute your ore with a large amount of waste, then your mill will not operate satisfactorily. Either high grade ore or very low grade ore or waste will upset the millhead and the mill will not work as satisfactorily as it will with the range of ore for which it was built.
In pointing out how gold mining assistance operates the hon. member used the figures that are in the book and I have no quarrel with those figures, but I think he realizes that what he was really saying was that he does not disagree with this system of high grading or low grading, that this is a good housekeeping proposition. I am suggesting that again he has forgotten something else that is prevalent throughout the whole gold mining industry and that is that the operators of the gold mining industry-and they are not very many in number-are eternal optimists. As the hon. member pointed out, in his area a number of the mines are controlled by one company. It is true that in each of the areas the people who are running and controlling the gold mining industry are eternal optimists when it comes to an increase in the price of gold. They operate for the day when the price of gold will go up. These people have been very surprised, because they were sure that when some of the present members of parliament who used to be outspoken champions of the gold mining industry when they were in opposition became supporters of a government they would continue to be champions of an increase in the price of gold. Now that they have become cabinet ministers, and some of them potential cabinet ministers they have not had the same desire to continually talk about an increase in the price of gold. Those people who are operating gold mines, being eternal optimists, are holding-and I am sure it is a fact-many sections of the well-known mines for the day when gold will be $70 an ounce.
While it is true that gold mining has to be maintained at the range for which the mill is designed to operate most efficiently, I still think some consideration should be given to this fact. There are people holding for themselves underground gold reserves against the day when the price of gold will rise. This is all we are asking the minister to check. We are not disagreeing that gold mines should be operated under what are called good housekeeping conditions, because we certainly support that. We agree entirely with what the hon. member has said. High grading is more detrimental to the country

and to the mining communities than low grading would be, but we think consideration must be given to some of the companies which are not totally dependent on emergency gold mining assistance, to see that they use the assistance to the best advantage of the communities.
Many of the smaller companies are in such a position that if emergency gold mining assistance were cut off or would require to be increased to an amount which the government would not see fit to recommend to maintain the small companies, they would be unable to operate. All we are suggesting is that the department of mines maintain continual surveillance of this problem so the money that is being paid to them in the form of a subsidy is used to the best advantage of the communities that are depending on this particular industry. When we make these charges in specific cases we are quite willing to give the names and the numbers of the stopes to the minister if he will give us some assurance that this information will not be neglected and that there will be an investigation. If we are wrong we shall be quite happy to get up in the House of Commons and say we were wrong in that particular instance.

As far as my constituency is concerned, I know the great importance of the excellent work done in connection with the Columbia basin survey since 1945. I do want to emphasize this, because I have received some comments from correspondents and I am afraid that through misunderstanding the nature of the report there may be a tendency to suggest that the staff has not been up to snuff. I have one or two suggestions to make before I sit down. The report suggests the expenditure of a good many millions of dollars, and I am a bit cautious when it comes to spending money. What little I have managed to gather here and there has been the result of hard labour. I was brought up in a home where my mother and father emphasized three things. They were opposed to injustice, opposed to dishonesty, and against waste. It is on that last point that I wish to speak. When the government is giving consideration to the recommendations in the report I suggest that there should be a survey of the work being undertaken in the mining, mapping and other branches of the various provincial governments and also in private industry, to make sure that in extending the staff there is no unnecessary duplication of effort and waste of funds.

The federal government are involved because they pay the subsidy. The provincial governments are involved because they administer their mining acts, and the municipal governments are certainly involved because they are very keenly and vitally interested in the life and health of these mining operations. At that time it will be coming up again for renewal or amendment or whatever action may be deemed advisable. Mr. Chairman, I do not like to take too much of the time of the committee, but I wish to say something on the price of gold. The price of gold is now based on the United States dollar, and over the past few years the government has been paying for an ounce of gold prices varying from $33.25 to $34, much lower than the price of $35 in Canadian money. This makes for a difficult situation.
Of course the previous and present governments have been very generous toward the industry and with good reason. The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act has done a lot of good for the gold mines. Last year the act was extended and the benefits to the gold mines increased by 25 per cent. However, in view of the fact that today gold is sold on the free market and people can hold gold here in Canada, which is a good thing because it has given some encouragement to the industry, the government is buying less gold. I think the government is buying very little gold produced by those mines which cannot benefit under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
For this reason I believe the government would be wise to buy all gold produced in this country, and for it should pay $35 Canadian to the producers, whether they are base metal mines or gold mines. Of course, they should continue the assistance to gold mines which can qualify under the act.
Now, if the government were to pay $35 an ounce in Canadian dollars they would encourage the base metal mines, and they would encourage mining in Canada. I would suggest that the government raise the price of gold, but this is a difficult problem; I understand that. This is an international question. Of course if the government of Canada were to raise the price of gold, let us say to $50, they would be paying a subsidy of $15 because all we could get for that gold if we were to sell it would be $35 in United States currency. However, I think the time will come when it will be a good thing for the government to raise the price of gold. If we were to raise the price of gold I am sure South Africa would follow our example and raise the price as well. In the meantime, I suggest we pay $35 in Canadian currency for the gold produced in this country, and that we continue the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act as it is.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in support of the lignite coal industry of Saskatchewan, and especially on behalf of the Great West Coal Company and the Saskatchewan Coal Company Limited, operating in the Estevan area in my constituency of Moose Mountain. The problem to which I am about to refer arises as a result of the 17 per cent freight rate increase last December. I feel that I should protest against the exclusion of lignite coal from the subsidy relief proposed by Bill No. C-38, and ask for relief against the increase in rates of 22 cents per ton on lignite coal authorized by order No. 96300 of the board of transport commissioners for the following reasons.
First, the lignite industry is faced with fierce competition from the new natural gas industry in its principal markets, and its very existence is threatened by the drastic price increases and anticipated loss of business to natural gas resulting from the freight rate increase.
Second, the lignite industry has not received any benefit from subventions comparable with that conferred on other branches of the Canadian coal industry.
In the third instance, lignite coal is a low value commodity subject to a comparatively short haul, but has received no relief from any of the successive flat per ton increases imposed on all coal in post-war years.
I should like to give a brief description of this industry in our area. Lignite coal is strip mined near Bienfait, Saskatchewan. A fairly constant production of slightly over 2,200,000 tons has been maintained since 1950. The principal markets are for industrial uses in the Winnipeg area. More than 70 per cent of the coal sold in the Winnipeg area is lignite. Other markets are in the Regina and Brandon areas, and certain pulp and paper plants at
6224	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
Kenora, Dryden and Fort Frances in Ontario. Lignite coal possesses a substantial market advantage as a low cost fuel located near its principal markets, only 280 miles from Winnipeg and 155 miles from Brandon.
In the post-war years the domestic house heating market has been pre-empted by fuel oil and latterly, to some extent, by natural gas. The industry by vigorous salesmanship, which included assistance to industrial users in the installation of proper heating plants, was able to develop an industrial market more than replacing the lost domestic market.
Concurrently the companies have invested more than $5 million in new equipment since the war. As a result of mechanization and technological improvements, the industry has been able to absorb successive wage increases, and has raised the mine price of coal by only 10 cents per ton since 1948. The present mine price averages $2 per ton.
I wish to compliment the minister, who I believe visited my constituency not too long ago and addressed an organization representing the coal industry there. The reports I received from the constituency indicate that the minister left a very good impression with them. I trust that he came away from that area in Saskatchewan with a favourable impression of it. While there I believe he inspected the operation of the machine known as Mr. Klimax, one of the largest strip mining machines on the North American continent, which is of assistance in rendering more economical the mining done there to have the product compete with other competitive fuels.
The lignite industry by its vigorous salesmanship and technological initiative has been able to maintain its position notwithstanding the competition of premium fuels in the postwar years. Its existence is now threatened by drastic increases in transportation expenses which it is powerless to control.
Another interesting sidelight in the lignite picture is that its position is good and will continue that way as long as industry survives. Expert studies such as the Gordon commission report agree that the outlook for Saskatchewan lignite is satisfactory. It is a low cost fuel located near industrial markets. Of particular importance is the growing demand for thermal power. Saskatchewan lignite is in a position to satisfy the demands of large thermal power stations erected or to be erected by Manitoba hydro at Brandon and Selkirk. If transportation costs can be held in check, lignite could supply the thermal power in these installations in preference to natural gas. On the other hand, even though the long term demand for lignite might be assumed to be satisfactory, it will avail little if the producing companies are not able to maintain
[Mr. Southam.I

their present markets and survive to enjoy it.
However, with reference to natural gas, which has sprung up in the area just in the last two years, since the greater part of the lignite market is industrial it is extremely vulnerable to the competition of natural gas. It is a well known feature of the natural gas industry that gas is offered for sale to industrial users at low prices in order to build up volume in a new natural gas pipe line or distributing system. As and when higher prices in the domestic markets are developed, low priced gas ceases to be available for industrial users. All proper steps should be taken to prevent the lignite industry from being destroyed by the initial competition of natural gas so it can survive to enjoy the brighter future which expert opinion predicts is in store for it.
Already some large accounts have switched from lignite coal to natural gas. As an example, one paper mill representing something like 5 per cent of the industry's total production has been lost. The industry could not survive many losses of this order. While the lignite industry is fighting to maintain its position, its competitive strength is gravely weakened by uncontrollable increases in transportation costs. The last 22 cents per ton increase is the equivalent of almost 2 cents per m.f.c. of natural gas. The failure of the lignite industry at this critical stage to obtain any relief from the recent increases will, it is feared, have an adverse effect on its customers and further strengthen natural gas competition.
Subventions do not apply to major lignite coal movements. This is something I was surprised to find out. While the lignite industry supports the aid extended to other branches of the coal industry in the form of subventions, it receives little assistance itself. In round figures, only 275,000 tons out of the total of 2,200,000 tons produced by the lignite industry benefit from subventions. The amount paid to the lignite industry was $247,000, or less than 85 cents per ton, subject to subvention. This is the tonnage delivered to pulp and paper mills in northwestern Ontario. The bulk of the industry's sales, which occur in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, do not qualify for subvention.
The substantial subventions paid to other branches of the coal industry have been referred to as one reason for not extending the benefit of the freight rate subsidy act to coal. The Minister of Transport on April 9, 1959, referred to subventions as follows, at page 2394 of Hansard:
Assistance to coal and coke is given in the form of subventions, and to show how those subventions have been increased, for instance, during the past two years, I will give the comparative figures

for the years 1956 and 1958. In 1956 the average subvention paid per ton was $2.67. In 1958, the average subvention per ton was $3.15. This shows that there has been an increase of 48 cents per ton during those two years, or an increase of 18 per cent.
Subventions paid during the calendar year 1958, by regions were as follows: In the maritime regions, that is in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, the amount was $8,546,041. In the western region, that is the province of Alberta and the Crowsnest area of British Columbia, the amount was $667,000.
On March 17 last the Prime Minister announced in the house that the federal government would pay an additional $500,000 in the form of subsidies to maritime coal this year. The government also recently announced the payment of an additional 50 cents per ton on 100,000 tons of Alberta coal which was being shipped to Japan, and this additional subvention was paid to make possible the sale of that quantity of coal.
The extent of present and future subsidies payable for maritime, Alberta and British Columbia coal overshadows the small subventions paid on lignite coal. In addition, the average subvention paid per ton is more than three times greater than the subvention paid on the small tonnage of lignite coal subject to subvention.
It would seem unfair to deny one branch of the coal industry relief from freight rate increases because of the special subventions paid to another branch. Moreover, it might appear advisable in the national interest to attempt to maintain the lignite industry in a reasonably sound economic position by the extension of the general freight rate subsidy to it. This alternative would appear more attractive than attempting later to shore up a near broken industry by subventions and other measures of special relief.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the last freight rate increase may be the straw that will break the camel's back in that particular part of the coal industry, and I am quite familiar with the problem because I have been working on it. I would strongly urge the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to give the problem of the Saskatchewan lignite coal industry very serious consideration.

We hope this will be carried out by this company, and that with the co-operation of all those upper Canadian markets, particularly the thermal plant in those areas, will be covered. If the company is a responsible one I believe that the government of Nova Scotia will help in the endeavour.
I have gone over the act providing for assistance to producers of coal in Canada and have looked into the matter as a lawyer, but I am not quite sure whether or not it covers new mines, in any event, if a competent company comes forward I believe that this government, on the basis of the submission of the government of Nova Scotia and the submission of the company, will certainly amend the act to make it possible for the company to obtain money to carry out this project. A new mine in the Westville area has been talked about for a long time and submissions have been made by the industrial committee within the area which includes representatives of business, labour and various other groups. At the last convention of the United Mine workers of America held in Truro a recommendation was made that a new mine be established in Pictou county.
A submission was made by the Canadian Labour Congress, accompanied by officers of the independent unions at Greenwood in Pictou county and the Drummond mine at Westville for the opening of a new mine. I recall that I spoke on this matter at I believe the first session of parliament which I attended which commenced in October, 1957. I repeat that any commission or investigation must look into the matter of coal mining particularly in the Atlantic area by considering a long range program and also looking into the situation of the independent producers in Pictou county and throughout the province of Nova Scotia. I would point out that formerly we had roughly 2,000 employees working in the coal industry in our county and today we have approximately 500 employed in three mines.
I should like to state that we appreciate very much the help given by the federal government as shown in the estimates for the Atlantic provinces thermal power plan, and a large extension of the thermal plant at Trenton in Pictou county has been in progress for some time. I notice in the press that the grid system between the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is now being completed and I hope that as more

power is used more coal will be used, particularly in the thermal plant in my own area. The idea when the legislation was passed at the first session in 1957 was to provide cheaper power for new industry and thus help the coal industry.
Other industries are being introduced in our area and at various other places in the province of Nova Scotia but it will take time and effort to attain the necessary objectives of the plan. I would submit and recommend that the coal industry must be preserved for the sake of the families and the communities of those areas where coal mining has decreased over a number of years. We must preserve our present industries as well as introduce new ones.
Finally, the minister visited my area and the province of Nova Scotia generally last year. He travelled around and saw the bankheads although he did not go down in the mines. He spoke to officials and labour in Pictou county and has first-hand information about the problem. I know that he will give every consideration to the recommendations and suggestions I have made.

I should like to say one more word. While no one on this side objected and, indeed, we supported the increase in the subventions to help meet the crisis in the coal industry, it does seem to me that the constructive way to deal with the long term coal problem is certainly not to pay large sums out of the treasury to transport coal to central Canada in order to build up industry in central Canada. If these large sums of public money are going to require to be spent over any long period, and I am sure they will be over quite a period, in order to maintain and ultimately to improve this industry, it seems to me there are two much better channels into which the money could be directed and I hope that the inquiry will look into this matter.
The first is the use of coal right at the pithead to develop power so that more industry can be located in these Atlantic provinces. The second is to accelerate research as I think we should have done when we were in office. I say that quite openly, but the fact that it was not done is no excuse for not getting ahead with it now. Last year was a highly profitable one for the British Columbia fishermen and also produced satisfactory results for most sectors of the Atlantic coast industry. The brightest feature of the Pacific coast industry was the near record catch of sockeye salmon. This came to 74 million pounds, worth $20 million. There had been high hopes for the dominant Adams river run, but even the most optimistic predictions of the scientists were surpassed. The total pack of canned sockeye was 1,100,000 48-pound cases and this was just short of the all-time record made in 1905. The Newfoundland bait service left something to be desired this year and last year and the matter of the availability of lobster bait this year in many parts of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick caused concern at the start of the season. The loss of fish export
had adverse effects on the fisheries of that province. I feel that I should state here, however, that markets are primarily the responsibility of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Nevertheless, that fact should not lessen the efforts of the Department of Fisheries in respect of markets for fish.
The minister's statement before the marine and fisheries committee gave a resume of existing conditions which assisted materially in the discussions of that committee. In passing, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I wonder why the word "marine" appears in the title of the committee on fisheries. Having regard to the many and varied problems that face the Department of Fisheries, both new ones and continuing ones

some which require negotiation with other countries, others that are complicated as between provinces; also problems within local fishing areas-the minister and his officials both here in Ottawa and in the field are, I am sure, deserving of appreciation and credit for their efforts and their desire to bring about the best possible solution under existing circumstances and in many cases complex aspects.
My opening remarks prompt me to state once again-and this is a personal view- that the status of the Department of Fisheries should be raised. The departmental estimates should be increased toward accelerating and expanding this most important department of government. As conditions and markets change in other industries, so do conditions and markets change in the primary industry of fisheries. These changes demand more research, better methods of processing and marketing, better methods of production, if we are to produce a product that will warrant higher prices to the trade and at the same time mean a saving to the consumer and a better price to the primary producer.
While efforts to cut down costs in the departmental estimates are commendable and pleasing I am sure to the Minister of Finance in this period of deficit financing, costs should not be cut down on phases of the department's work that require expansion to improve the industry. As the Atlantic provinces' outlook as an industrial area does not appear to hold very bright prospects, emphasis should be placed on fishing and farming in order to help stabilize the economy of these provinces. I trust that the minister will be able to convince his cabinet colleagues, particularly the Minister of Finance, that there is a vital necessity and expediency for an increased share of public moneys to do the complete job for fisheries that is necessary as a safeguard for the industry's future.

Supply-Fisheries
It does not take a northern vision to realize what is necessary for the future of the fishing industry. Canada's oldest primary producer has not kept pace with rapid advances throughout the years to the same extent as other industries particularly in terms of financial income to the primary producers and the methods of production and marketing.
In this year's main estimates the total vote for the Department of Fisheries is $19,544,777, a decrease of approximately $269,554 from last year's main estimates. The supplementary estimates recently tabled include further items in the amount of $1,788,090. It is encouraging to note that further moneys will be provided for economics services, industrial development and for conservation services. I trust that there is no sizeable decrease in moneys for essential services this year. If there has been a decrease in any of these votes, outside the major projects mentioned by the minister in the marine and fisheries committee, I ask the minister if he will advise the committee where decreases were made and why.
There is a phase of the department's work about which I wish to make some remarks. The many reports heard from maritime sources-reports heard from reliable fishermen with long experience in both commercial and sport fishing-leave the impression that an exhaustive survey should be made towards instituting a better program of protection and conservation. I am sure the department is aware of this situation and probably has considered plans to extend the present program but is not able to do so because sufficienl moneys are not voted by parliament.
The additional information gathered by an exhaustive survey, together with information now in the possession of the department, could be the basis for a comprehensive study of an adequate conservation and protective system. In this connection I make particular reference to conservation and protection for the propagation of salmon and lobster.
The department's staff in the field directed by officials at Ottawa is doing a good job in so far as a good job can be done by a staff inadequate in number. There are many miles of water to patrol, many spawning areas to protect, which cannot be adequately patrolled and protected by a staff that is too few in numbers.
Mr. Chairman, at this time may I make brief reference to the plans of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources for very large additions to its staff for expansion in Canada's northland. It is my firm conviction that the development of Canada's oldest industry-fisheries-should hold priority over the development of a part

of our country which is sparsely inhabited, and that the inherent rights of those Canadians and their ancestors who have made a great contribution to the building up of this country should not be disregarded when consideration is given to the financial assistance necessary to place the fishing industry on the highest possible plane. The development of Canada's northland is essential. However, it should be developed in accordance with a long range plan to be brought about when the ills of our populated areas have been solved, not at the expense of other parts of the country.
These last remarks, Mr. Chairman, bring me back to something which I have been promoting for years-the need for an expansion in all branches of the Department of Fisheries. The assistance given by governments to western wheat and grain farmers is well known and, may I add, not always understood by people in other parts of Canada. It has been criticized on the basis that similar assistance in a comparable degree is not provided for other primary producers.
I stated previously that the total amount to be voted for the Department of Fisheries in the main estimates for the year 1959-60 is $19,544,777. In comparison it will be noted that according to the figures in the estimates book there are 20 other departments of government which will be voted more moneys than the Department of Fisheries. These votes range from $21 million to $1,750 million. For example, the estimates of the Department of Agriculture amount to $106 million, and here are some other figures: Atomic Energy $32 million; Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, $70 million; national research council, $30 million; northern affairs and national resources, $85 million. As I say, the expenditure is topped by the Department of National Defence with a vote of $1,750 million.
Mr. Chairman, if the members of this house representing constituencies which have fishing interests would join together in an attempt to raise the status of the Department of Fisheries to its proper level and ensure that moneys were made available to do all the things which could and should be done to improve our fishing industry, then a notable service would be performed in the best interests of our country and in the interest of an industry which is essential not only to our national economy but also to the health of our nation.
There are three matters I wish to draw to the attention of the minister at this time. They do not come completely within the jurisdiction of the minister, but they are of direct concern to the fishing industry and in consequence I judge my references to them to be in order under the general item

now under discussion. On June 5, when the estimates of the Public Works Department were before the committee. I requested the Minister of Public Works to have a complete survey made of Miramichi waters in preparation for the construction of small landings and improved facilities, in addition to dredging, to assist the Miramichi fishing industry. At that time I urged the minister to seek the co-operation of the Minister of Fisheries in this task, and I now ask the Minister of Fisheries to make representations with a view to having this survey made. May I suggest, also, that the survey be a physical, on the spot survey, and that information be obtained from fishermen actively engaged in the industry as to the need for facilities. I suggest, also, that the economic branch of the Department of Public Works should not look on these suggested small projects with a jaundiced eye of a hard-shell banker, but that other factors be considered besides the actual dollar return on the costs, because these small landings and other improved facilities will increase the over-all volume and value of the fishery and in a short time results will prove that the expenditures were warranted, to say nothing of the fact that the hard task of the fisherman will in some measure have been alleviated.
Another subject that I wish to raise concerns loans under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Earlier this session when the bill to extend the life of this act was before the house suggestions were made that more extensive advertising should be undertaken in order to acquaint fishermen of the provisions of this measure. I trust that the officials of the fisheries department have urged the Department of Finance to conduct a wider advertising campaign in this regard. I hold in my hand a pamphlet issued under the imprint of the Queen's printer. It outlines the procedure to be followed in making application for the loan, and the last subheading in the pamphlet reads: "See the manager of your local bank or credit union". I had personal experience in this connection in the course of efforts to assist certain fishermen with their applications for loans, and I found that local bank managers had very little knowledge of the act and still less of the regulations, for the reason that they had never been furnished with pamphlets or other data. As a result valuable time was spent in securing clarification from the Department of Finance and from federal fisheries officials.
On the basis of this experience I judge that the same situation exists in many localities, or that it did exist, and I strongly urge that steps be taken, if they have not already been taken since the recent request 66968-9-395
Supply-Fisheries
was made, to forward to banks and credit unions in fishing areas complete information in both official languages about this act.
I wish also to solicit the minister's support of amendments at the next session to increase the repayment period permissible for loans under this act for the purchase or construction of fishing equipment, and I urge the hon. gentleman to make representations along these lines to the Minister of Finance. I hope the act may be amended so that instead of the present three-year repayment term we may be able to take advantage of a graduated plan of repayments over a period up to eight years depending upon the amount of the loan requested. This period of up to eight years is suggested because certain other loans under this act are linked with an eight-year repayment period.
It is not my intention to discuss at this time local aspects of Miramichi fisheries. In the past I have placed certain views on the record. I have discussed local matters with the officials of the departments and I shall have further discussions and correspondence as representations reach me from Miramichi fishermen's association and other interested groups. However, there are two questions about which I wish to make a comment at this time in regard to telegrams which I have received. On July 15 I received the following telegram from the chairman of the fishermen's association:
Miramichi salmon drift net fishermen are disappointed that after recent disaster lift period was not eliminated but just rotated which is no direct assistance. Drifters now request they be allowed to fish through to August 15 as requested by prior representation from this association. Copy of this wire sent to Hon. Angus MacLean and Hon. R. Pichette. Sgd. H. G. Crocker, chairman.
I also received a telegram this afternoon in this connection. It is dated July 17, and reads as follows:
Drifters would like you to remind minister setting back of lift period was suggestion of private individual and not their request or that of Hon. Mr. Pichette. With mackerel a failure next two weeks looks grim for these men. Sgd. H. G. Crocker.
I wish now to make reference to the representations recently made by the Miramichi commercial fishermen's association for the advancement of the opening date of the Miramichi smelt fishing season to October 15 from the present date of October 30. I know the minister will give sympathetic consideration to these matters. I appreciate the problems he faces in the conservation of the fisheries. We realize that conservation is of prime importance. I know that the fishermen of Miramichi have an understanding of

Supply-Fisheries
his difficulties and they know that whatever decision the minister reaches will be arrived at on sound grounds.
I trust that the future holds a general improvement in the fishing industry and that the Department of Fisheries will get a larger share of the public purse next year to carry out the improvements that are needed and that our lost fish export markets will be regained and new ones promoted.
I wish now to comment on the tragic storm of June 20 that took the lives of 35 Miramichi salmon fishermen and caused extensive damage including the loss of boats and nets and considerable damage to lobster traps. Of the 35 men and boys who lost their lives 13 are accounted for and 22 are still missing. There were several family groups among the fatalities including fathers, sons and brothers. Eighty-three children have been left fatherless. Twenty widows with 83 children have been left with no means of livelihood. Four mothers who were previously dependent on their sons are now left without support. They face a bleak future until their children come of age and can provide support.
A disaster fund is being raised from subscriptions. On behalf of the families and the district I wish to express appreciation for the donations that have been made. The care of the widows and their children will be a continuing problem for many years to come and it is hoped that the disaster fund will reach the required amount.
With regard to assistance for the replacement of boats, salmon nets and lobster traps, I believe this assistance should be provided by the federal and provincial governments at the earliest possible time so the fishermen can get back into the industry at the former level of production.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs, New Brunswick's representative in the federal cabinet, when expressing his sympathy over the tragic storm, said in part as reported at page 4988 of Hansard of June 22:
-everything possible will be done to see that help is given these needy families in the way of restoring equipment and gear.
These were most welcome words which helped to ease the feeling of the stricken families that all was lost.
On June 30, as reported at page 5269 of Hansard of that date, I asked the Minister of Fisheries if any plans had been formulated to date toward rendering assistance to Miramichi salmon drifters and lobster fishermen. In reply the minister stated in part that the department provides a subsidized insurance system for fishermen with regard to boats and lobster traps. The minister also stated

that in many cases he believed insurance was carried and that in cases where insurance was not carried, that in the event of a disaster of this type the first responsibility rested with the provincial level of government. The minister qualified this statement by saying:
I am sure that any requests which may come through that channel for assistance would be very sympathetically considered by this government.
It therefore appears that the federal government will assess damages and make payments where insurance was carried and will give consideration to assistance for loss and damage where no insurance coverage was carried upon request from the government of the province of New Brunswick. It is my contention that both levels of government should provide assistance for losses suffered as has been done in other cases and that the disaster fund raised by public subscriptions should not have to be used to replace boats, nets and lobster traps.
The present situation among the salmon drift net and lobster fishermen of the south shore of the Miramichi bay is grim and bleak. Most of the fishermen were in debt for their boats and nets prior to the storm and if assistance is not forthcoming they will be burdened with larger debt and in many cases may not be able to secure the credit to purchase new equipment. Most of the boats, nets _ and lobster traps that were salvaged are m need of extensive repairs which add to the burden of debt.
If no request has been received to date from the provincial government I appeal to the minister to take immediate steps to contact the provincial government with respect to working out a plan of assistance, as it is vital that no time be lost in deciding what joint action will be taken. These primary producers should be rendered assistance in their hour of need. Hon. members of this committee and Canadians generally are familiar with other forms of assistance granted by the federal government on a great number of occasions in cases where the need was not as great and without attendant tragic circumstances as in this instance.
Preliminary reports disclose that out of 53 boats lost in the Miramichi bay-Northum-berland strait area, 23 were covered by insurance under the fishermen's indemnity plan. At this time I do not have the actual number of boats of the Escuminac fleet that were lost and were not covered by insurance but I feel safe in assuming that more than half would not have been covered.
A greater loss in terms of dollar value was suffered in the loss and damage of lobster traps on which, unfortunately, no

insurance was carried. As nets were not insurable under the indemnity plan, a complete loss was suffered on this type of gear. The nets that were salvaged sustained a 50 per cent loss of value and subsequent length of time of usage over and above the cost of repairs.
A temporary formula to provide for the immediate needs of the stricken families has been set up and disbursements are being made from the publicly subscribed relief fund. A permanent formula will be drafted when the total amount of the fund is known. Much more money is needed and further appeals are being made to provide the necessities of life for the widows and children, both for the immediate future and in the years ahead. On their behalf I appeal to the generosity of all who can make contributions, large or small, to do so. Donations will be accepted at any branch of the Royal Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am very sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I am obliged to tell him that his time has expired.
I have only two or three more sentences, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it the wish of the committee to give unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I appreciate the indulgence of the committee. Since the tragic storm, requests have been made for adequate aids to navigation and for an improved system of reporting the weather and in particular advancing storms. The Minister of Transport has given me assurance that he will look into this matter immediately. Many such improvements can be made in the fishing area of Miramichi bay, improvements that would prevent loss of life, the lack of which was brought out so dramatically on June 20.
It is also pleasing to note that the provincial government officials have taken action toward gaining recognition for the acts of heroism that were performed by the fishermen. The acting premier of New Brunswick, the Hon. Mr. Skaling, has already made efforts in this direction.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I again wish to express my deepest heartfelt sympathy to the bereaved families, and I trust divine providence and sympathetic support in some measure will help them in their time of great sorrow, not only in a spiritual way but also in a material way.
I also wish once again on behalf of the constituents I represent to express appreciation to all those who assisted in the search 66968-9-3954
Supply-Fisheries
and rescue and to all those who made contributions to the disaster fund; also a special word of appreciation to Her Majesty the Queen and Prince Philip for the gift they made to this fund. It is pleasing to note that arrangements are being made to transport the widows an dtheir children to Pointe du Chene, New Brunswick, to meet the Queen. At that time she can add a personal note of expression to her previous message of condolence.
I wish to end, Mr. Chairman, on a note expressing the hope that nothing will be left undone in the humanitarian efforts that must be put forth by both governments and all others who are able to assist, so that efforts will not be found wanting, efforts that will forever have the deepest appreciation of the bereaved families and all the people of the stricken area.

Mr. Chairman, first on behalf of the C.C.F. representation in the house- I am sure I am speaking with a unanimous voice on this occasion, anyway-I would like to express our appreciation not only of the manner in which the minister has been able to grasp the vastly complex problems within the department but of the genial and sincere way in which he always discusses the questions relating to his department. I have the greatest admiration for the minister in this regard. In his spare moments I think he might be able to find some extra curricular occupation by giving some guidance in this matter to such gentlemen as the Minister of Finance and other cabinet ministers. I should also like to express our appreciation of the attitude and of the work conducted by the members of the minister's staff, the scientists, biologists and others who work unceasingly for the promotion of fisheries questions and for the development of our fisheries in Canada and for the consumption of fish by Canadians and others.
As the minister said, these departmental estimates were dealt with rather extensively in the committee, but as I mentioned to the minister when I met him in the corridor one day, he should have arranged to bring his estimates before the house as soon as the committee was over and he would have got them through right away. The longer the delay the more problems arise that require additional discussion.
I should like to make reference to two or three specific matters, and in the process pose some questions to the minister. In the committee's proceedings, if I can make reference to one or two pages as a preface, on Friday, April 10, at page 45, following some discussion about the knowledge of trawlers and other fishing vessels from the

Private Bills
Soviet union which were sighted out in the Pacific and so on, the minister had this comment to make:
Mr. Chairman, the department has some information regarding Russian trawlers that are now fishing in the Bering sea. Reports indicate that there are about 42 trawlers, six refrigeration ships, a tug and a transport.
Farther on he said:
As yet, we have no indication that this Russian fleet is fishing any types of fish that are covered by any treaties now in effect.
I have some special interest here in so far as the salmon fisheries are concerned, because it is known there is an intermingling area out in that particular area where the Soviet trawlers were noticed. Can the minister give us any additional information about the activities of those particular Soviet ships that were sighted out in the Bering sea and in other parts? Can he give us the information he has at the moment which might be additional to that which he gave to the committee on April 10? However, there is a problem which might arise out of the activities of fishing vessels in so far as our salmon fisheries on the west coast are concerned? A problem might arise out of fishing vessels which belong to countries which are not signatories to the north Pacific fisheries treaty, such as are Japan, the United States and Canada, if the Soviet union is fishing in waters far from its own shores. Even though at the moment it may not be fishing for fish that we in British Columbia are concerned with; nevertheless the possibility is there because of technological changes and the size of the fish that the Soviet fishermen can take out in the fishing areas which are now restricted to fishing by the Pacific fisheries commission. It is five o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
