AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was at this point in my speech. At the time of our visit 600 people were on the payroll; however, when the heavy run on smelts was over, the staff would be greatly reduced. The operations would then be confined to yellow perch and what pickerel would be available along with all rough fish that would be suitable for mink food.
The greater part of the production of this plant is marketed in the United States and delivery is made by their own transports. They related to us that they were unable to supply the demand for their smelts and were hoping to devise means of taking them throughout the fishing season. At present their equipment is designed to take them in their opening run when they congregate in schools.
This expedition was a revelation to the whole committee. Expressions of satisfaction and appreciation were much in evidence. The

members from the coastal regions gained a knowledge of our inland waters that will be advantageous at future deliberations on our great lakes fisheries problems. Furthermore, they will carry back to the coastal fisheries some new ideas in respect to modern processing equipment developed at the Olmstead plant. The opportunity to make such observations and to exchange views on biology and conservation with experts, who were included in our party, was invaluable to all concerned. A good representation of the fisheries of lake Erie met with the committee and their spokesman graciously expressed the gratitude of his colleagues for our efforts and interest in their welfare.
The absence on this trip of all of our committee members from the opposition parties appeared to be intentional. Especially was this indicated when the hon. member from Ottawa West, in hope of gaining some political advantage, on the following day questioned the Minister of Fisheries as to what department supplied the transportation and who paid for the trip. The members of the committee who failed to avail themselves of the opportunity to see some of the most modern fish processing equipment in the world, did the fishermen they represent a real injustice. They could have been in a position to pass on to them valuable knowledge.
My immediate concern in speaking to these estimates is, of course, the Georgian bay and lake Huron. This has been a great fish producing body of water, where many of my constituents operated commercially and prospered; however, for reasons stated earlier in these observations, commercial and game fish cease to exist in quantities that make it worth while for fishermen to continue in the industry, and the lake trout, as a tourist attraction, has been nullified. My foremost purpose on the marine and fisheries committee is to use my influence in promoting the early restoration of lake trout and whitefish or other suitable fish to the Georgian bay and lake Huron. In their productive years, the three largest great lakes, Superior, Michigan and Huron, produced 15 million pounds of lake trout annually. Now this is dwindling toward zero.
It has been ascertained that lamprey seldom kill fish under 20 inches in length; therefore, I suggest that more emphasis be placed on the production of splake, a cross between lake and speckled trout, which reaches maturity and would start a reproductive cycle before attaining the size which is suitable for attack by lamprey. Many of the now idle fish hatcheries could help in speeding up this restocking program in respect to splake and perhaps on other suitable species.
Supply-Fisheries
On the week end, I made a survey of fish hatcheries in my district and two out of three have been idle for four years. The third one, the Wiarton hatchery, is operating at only 30 per cent of its capacity, producing lake trout for stocking lake Simcoe. This situation would perhaps apply to other hatcheries as well. I am aware that these hatcheries are provincial property, but I feel sure the federal Department of Fisheries or the conservation commission would be permitted to make use of all available facilities. We in the great lakes area would most certainly like to see a restoration of lake trout and whitefish; nevertheless, a lot of time should not be lost while we entertain a wait and see attitude; therefore, I submit the following information for further consideration. It has been demonstrated on several occasions that fish could be transferred to new surroundings successfully.
In checking over reports of the researchers, I note that in 1929 Dymond, Hart and Pritchard report the establishment of sea-run populations of spring salmon in the St. John river in New Brunswick and Port Credit river in Ontario. These salmon have been taken in the St. John river by the hundreds and vary in weight up to eight pounds. Fish up to 30 pounds have been taken from the Port Credit river. The streams and coastal regions of Maine, New Brunswick and Ontario are the only foreign waters on the North American continent in which natural populations of Pacific salmon have been established; however, it appears now that these salmon have disappeared from lake Ontario.
I think the researchers would agree that lake Ontario was not an ideal body of water for this experiment. The lake lacked a good depth of water and many of the streams flowing into it could not be considered much more than open sewers. In recent years this condition has been cleared up to a large extent with the development of sewage and waste disposal plants. Georgian bay and lake Huron, with their cold deep water, continually replenished from scores of clean streams, offer ideal conditions for the introduction of Pacific salmon. At this point I will make some further observations in respect to the introduction of Pacific salmon south of the equator.
The Tasmania fisheries commission in 1933 stated that, in the confined water of their great lake, spring salmon thrive and grow rapidly to support a flourishing sport fishery. Sockeye salmon introduced to lake Ohau in New Zealand have acquired a landlocked habit. These fish run up creeks at the head of the lake and spawn there every year in March and April.

Supply-Fisheries
The sea-run population of Pacific salmon that have been successfully established in both Chile and New Zealand have adjusted their life cycle to the change in occurrence of the seasons in the southern hemisphere. The spawning migrations of these salmon occur in January, February and March, which are seasonal equivalents of July, August and September in the northern hemisphere.
Much progress and many improvements have been made in fish cultural methods in recent years which should help in securing desired results in transplanting of sockeye or spring salmon to the great lakes. I make these observations to support my conviction that salmon can be successfully reared and propagated in the upper lakes.
I suggest to the minister that an experiment to introduce some of the coastal waters salmon to the upper great lakes be conducted at the earliest convenience and that some of the money paid to the international conservation commission be designated for this purpose. The sockeye salmon from the west coast and spring salmon from the east coast have been able to reproduce and live with the sea lamprey and smelts. Would it not be reasonable to assume they could continue to live in this environment in the great lakes? Should this prove to be true, and the lamprey and smelts prove to be uncontrollable, this could be the solution to our problem. The introduction of fish to new environment may be very important to ensuring suitable production for sport and commercial fishing in our great lakes in the years ahead.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I emphasize that fishery conditions in lake Huron and Georgian bay have created a serious situation for all the fishermen depending on these waters for a livelihood. Their life earnings are tied up in fishing boats, docks and other gear, none of which is saleable. The tourist industry has suffered to lesser extent, yet worthy of note. Many tourist operators who had depended on the lake trout for an attraction just do not have anything to offer. For instance, Cape Croker on the Bruce peninsula was a location for ideal lake trout trolling. It brought thousands of dollars to the Indians on the Cape Croker reserve who rented their boats and acted as guides. It also meant much to camp operators who supplied the other accommodation necessary.
In the town of Meaford lake trout trolling was considered one of their best industries. At one time they had a fleet of forty or more pleasure craft built and designed for the purpose of trolling for lake trout. Today not a single boat leaves the harbour for the

purpose of trolling for trout. The chamber of commerce of this town estimate that this tourist business was worth one quarter of a million dollars to them. I have cited the experience of these localities with which I am familiar, but it applies to the whole lake Huron and Georgian bay area.
I am aware of the fact that some of the problems I mention are partly provincial responsibilities; however, I am anxious to see federal funds and influence work in full co-ordination with provincial effort to bring about the desired results and with some expediency.

I have no intention of holding up the estimates of the department nor do I intend to burden the committee with a history of the fishing industry and the woes and tribulations of the fishermen of my constituency. Those problems can be solved in co-operation with the minister and the officials of his department. But I think I would be most ungrateful if I did not bring to the attention of the committee the importance of this item as far as my constituency is concerned. We have in my constituency the largest sardine cannery in the British empire and the largest lobster pound in the world. These are the two important items of our fisheries. You can therefore see that investigation and research through the biological gation and research through the biological portant to the fishermen of my riding and also to the general economy of the constituency.
In June, 1959 the Minister of Fisheries opened a new wing to the biological station and commemorated 50 years of the service in biological research to the constituency. There is employed by the Department of Fisheries, according to the last report, that for 1957-58, a total of 25 boats in the province of New Brunswick with a crew of 106. There was spent on the biological boats alone $105,000 and there was spent on the boats engaged in protection in New Brunswick $150,000. In connection with work at the biological station there was spent during 1957-58, $475,000 and in the province of New Brunswick roughly $1,750,000. You can therefore see that this item is extremely important. I think that I would be very remiss if I did not express the appreciation of the fishermen of my constituency to the Minister of Fisheries and to his staff for their work in this regard.

Back in May I asked the minister if he would make a statement on the department's program dealing with the lamprey situation in the great lakes, especially in lake Superior. At that time he said that he would make a statement on the matter

when his estimates were before the house. I wonder whether he would do it now.

Yes. As all hon. members know, this is a very vast problem. Due to the invasion of lamprey in the great lakes or the infestation of the great lakes by the lamprey as a result of the manmade canals to the great lakes, the whole ichthyology of the lakes has been upset. The lamprey, which are a parasite, thrived in these waters where they never had existed in previously and where there are no natural predators on them.
This is a problem which we have been working at for a number of years now in co-operation with the United States and our agency that does the work under the international great lakes fishery commission, is the fisheries research board of Canada.
First this problem was attacked by trying to control the migration of the lamprey to streams up which they go to spawn by means of electrical barriers. Another approach that was tried concurrently was to find a specific poison for lampreys; and a break-through in this matter has been made in recent months. Two chemicals have been discovered which proved lethal or proved to be a selective poison for lampreys. In other words, in certain concentration it will destroy the lamprey and their larvae, which is important, but will not affect other forms of fish life. This year we are doing a trial project on a reasonably large scale poisoning certain of the streams. It is too early yet to judge what the result will be but it seems encouraging. I do not think there is any more I can say at the moment at this late point. But if there is any other information the hon. member for Algoma West or any other hon. member would like to have, I should be delighted to supply all details.
Item agree to.
515. Industrial development service - further amount required, $800,000.
This vote shows a fairly substantial amount of money. I wonder whether we could have from the minister an indication of what is entailed in this particular vote.

This is really a transfer from the Department of Public Works to the Department of Fisheries for the community stage program in Newfoundland which was introduced last fall partly as a winter work program.

Item agreed to.
Supply-Fisheries
519. Newfoundland bait service-further amount required, $101,000.

The matter of bait supply seems to be an annual problem. I certainly should like to mention my appreciation of the interest that the minister's department is taking in this problem in Newfoundland. What I want to mention now is the possibility of using artificial bait as a supplement to frozen bait. I mention this matter because the type of artificial lure which is used in sports fishing has been used with considerable success in catching cod. As a matter of fact, one man that I know who used the type of lure which is used, as I say, in sports fishing, in fishing side by side with fishermen using the ordinary type of jigger, was much more successful in landing his fish. I would suggest that perhaps the minister's department might look into the possibility of developing types of lures for cod fish similar to what the sports industry has for sports fishermen.

I am highly appreciative of the hon. member's suggestion. I can say that the fisheries research board has been doing some work on artificial baits of various kinds. In addition to that our industrial development branch has been doing trials on various types of lures. We are hoping that some solution to this problem may be found, because it would be a great relief not only to the department but also to a large number of fishermen who have difficulty in making sure there is a constant supply of bait. I must say, with reference to bait, that squid are in very short supply. They have not appeared as yet. But as an insurance measure we have fairly large holdings of other types of bait, so that we will not be destitute, as it were, if the squid fail to appear. We have some 1,750,000 pounds of bait in storage at the moment.
521. Destruction of dogfish and other predators, $250,000.

This item relates to the
destruction of dogfish and other predators. A similar amount was voted for this purpose in the supplementary estimates last session for the last fiscal year but I understand the program did not work out too well mostly because it was started too late in the season. I would certainly appreciate it if the minister could indicate whether this dogfish destruction program will start immediately and also on what basis they are going to use the fund. Perhaps the minister would indicate whether he hopes to use the entire vote this year instead of the small amount of this vote which was actually used last year.

Supply-Fisheries

Last year when this amount was voted it took a considerable length of time before we were able to reach agreement with everyone concerned as to a satisfactory program, and it was late in the season before the program got under way. It began at a time of the year which was perhaps not the best time for the catching of dogfish. But we will be in the position to announce the program immediately this vote is passed and this year we are paying a bounty, one might call it, of ten cents a pound on dogfish liver and we hope this will prove successful.
Is this money to be used solely for dogfish destruction or are there plans to deal with sea lions and so on?

There was a possibility when this vote was drawn that a small amount might be used for sea lion control but we have found a method of doing that under another vote, and this entire amount will be used against dogfish.
I may not be quite in order in asking this question on this item but I should like to know from the minister if land for the site of the bait unit at Bonne Bay and Woody Point has been secured?

As the hon. member knows, we had some difficulty in finding a suitable location for the bait unit at Bonne Bay but I believe I am correct in saying that recently we obtained a suitable site at Woody Point, and the unit was transferred there, or it is in the process of being transferred.
May I ask the minister whether sites have been chosen on the west coast of Newfoundland for any of the seven units which are being provided for in the present year?

There has been no final decision with regard to the eight units which are being provided for in this year's estimates. As the hon. member knows, there have been a large number of demands from a great number of areas, and we have to study the relative needs of all those areas, the possibility of other sources of supply and so forth. No final decisions have as yet been made as to the areas in which they will be set up.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That completes the estimates of the Department of Fisheries.

Mr. Chairman, if I may say so, I want first to correct one impression I may have left inadvertently with the committee. I may have sounded as if I believed that everything was rosy in the garden and that there were no problems as far as fishermen were concerned. That is not the case. There are areas, especially in connection with certain types of fish production, where the economics of the industry are not very good because the production is going to a low price market. I do not want to labour the point, but I have in mind such things as salt cod in Newfoundland and smoked herring-bloaters-in places such as the Magdalen islands. I want to assure the committee that these problems are under constant review, and we hope to find some way of improving the situation.
That is all I want to say at the moment, except to express my appreciation for the high degree of co-operation that the committee has shown to me and to my officials.
294. Departmental administration, including Canada's share of the upkeep of the international bureaux at Berne and Montevideo, $1,915,483.
I suppose that the Postmaster General has something very interesting to tell us. I will ask him now, very respectfully, to say something about this first item.

I thank the hon. member for St. Denis for inferring that this was going to be very interesting. I was hopeful, for a moment, that he might even accept the estimates of this department without hearing any comment whatsoever from the minister. But I am delighted to review briefly our operations over the past year and tell the committee something of what we are doing.
At the outset, I should like to pay my tribute to the people who operate the postal service, the department's 50,000 employees. Their quiet spirit of dedication, their sincerity and devotion to the job they do and their untiring labours are the foundation of Canada's postal service, and it is a strong, sure foundation of which Canadians may well be proud.
Because of this government's belief that the public is best served when its employees feel that there is an interest in their morale, their welfare and their working conditions, I am particularly encouraged by the general improvement in the morale of our service and

in the bettered relationships between our employee organizations and the administration which has occurred during the past two years.
Nowhere is this better illustrated than in the April editorial in the Postal Tribune, the official organ of the Canadian Postal Employees' Association, which dealing generally with changes and improvements we have introduced says in part:
While the change has been gradual, there is ample evidence that all changes have been to the benefit of the service (to the public) and the employees.
. . . Another change quite evident to officers and members of our organization is the present attitude of senior officials both at headquarters and in the field. In the past organizations were tolerated and in many cases co-operation was a one way street. The new era has made it more evident that problems presented by postal organization organizations should and will receive serious consideration in view of how such problems affect morale and staff efficiency.
With such a spirit it is easy to understand why the past fiscal year, and the months since then to the present, have been a period of further progress and achievement for the Post Office Department; a period during which we have made desirable improvements in service to the public which I shall detail in a few moments; during which we have introduced changes of benefit to our employees; and during which we have made plans and taken the initial steps which will be increasingly reflected in the months to come in further advances.
In this respect no single change is of greater importance than that introduced a few months ago with the establishment of our new engineering and development branch on a level equal in all respects with those other five branches into which postal service has traditionally been divided.
Before this new division of reponsibility, engineering and development was but one part of the work of the operations branch of the department. Faced with the multitudinous problems of directing the day to day operation of the postal service, and the pressing and immediate difficulties which continually arise when 10 million pieces of mail must be handled daily, that work which is the foundation of present and future postal improvements in Canada had often to be delayed and neglected in favour of the more immediate problems.
Now, headed by one of our most experienced postal officials and a man who has a particular capacity for this work, engineering and development has attained its proper status in our organization and this has already been reflected in the acceleration of many of our projects. The new branch has as its primary functions research in mechanization and postal techniques, examination of new ideas in postal
Supply-Post Office
operations developed in other areas; testing of new machines and techniques; a continual review of all standard postal equipment in order to improve its design; provision of mail handling equipment to post offices, and arrangements for buildings, space and facilities for carrying out all postal operations.
In the field of modernization, probably the most important single project is the development of an electro-mechanical mail sorting machine. This project, as many of you know, has been under research and development for some years and has now reached the stage where a contract has been awarded to Cana-dair Limited in Montreal for the construction of the first complete machine to be tested under operating conditions in a post office.
We also expect during the first half of 1960 to install and begin testing a machine which has been developed by the British post office for automatically culling and facing up letters, cancelling their stamps and separating them into local and out of town groups.
These two machines together provide for the mechanization of letter handling in a post office from the time the mail bag is opened until the letter is ready for forwarding to another city or a letter carrier for delivery. I have no doubt that a decade hence we shall look back on them as primitive-just as we now consider the model T Ford to have been a primitive form of automobile transportation-but the fact remains that we are breaking through that barrier which has made the postal service, not only of Canada but generally throughout the world, one of the least mechanized of all mass handling operations.
I should remind hon. members again, as I have in the past, that while such developments are likely to enable us to reduce our part-time staff-people who work three or four hours a day at peak periods in the post office-they are not likely to represent reductions in our present full time staff. Primarily we are seeking not a decrease in manpower but an improvement in our efficiency to allow us to deal without delay with our ever-increasing mail volume.
In addition to these devices we have forged ahead with other new technological innovations, many of which are now operating in our newer and larger post offices. We have developed numerous intricate and effective conveyor systems which speed up the handling of mail at our bigger offices and which reduce the number of man hours required to handle a piece of mail.
We have also developed in several cities experimental models of curbside mailing boxes for the use of the motoring public.

Supply-Post Office
These are redesigned parcel receptacles fitted with a funnel-shaped snorkel facing the street side. They may be used by a motorist without leaving his car. Generally speaking, these boxes have proved popular. The need for them was dictated by increasing city traffic and by a shortage of parking space in downtown areas.
I suppose it is a commentary on our way of life to report that having designed and installed boxes of this kind we are now being pressed to put them only on one-way streets so that a man may drive up and deposit mail in the box from the driver's side of the vehicle. If we put them on twoway streets there is the possibility that the driver may have to slide across the seat of the automobile in order to deposit the mail and in some cases people find that even that is too much.
I want to pay this tribute. We have had fine co-operation from civic authorities where we have set them up and 26 of the newly designed receptacles have been placed in service in various cities across the country. This type of installation will be expanded as suitable sites are determined.
In recent years the department has purchased and installed 1,500 new type stamp vending machines and purchase is planned of a further 500 during the next year. The machines are being installed at railway terminals, bus depots, hotel lobbies and outside post office buildings. They serve a dual purpose in that they tend to take some of the pressure off the regular wicket sale of stamps at peak hours and, more important, they are available to the mailing public 24 hours a day. These machines, you will note, give full face value in stamps for the money deposited.
We have undertaken a study of mail boxes and receptacles in use throughout the country with a view to reducing the variety of types in service. We expect to be able to effect substantial savings in the procurement and distribution of these boxes by standardizing sizes and types to a greater degree than in the past.
In our continuing program to streamline administrative operations we have installed an electronic punch card calculator at headquarters. This complex device will save thousands of man hours in processing post office savings bank accounts and in calculating salary payments to revenue postmasters. In addition, we are investigating other uses to which this device can be put which will materially reduce the costs in time and money of routine clerical operations.
We are also making extensive studies in the handhng of money orders with a view to

developing a system based on electronic accounting machines similar to those being developed for use by financial institutions which should considerably streamline our operations in this field.
Some evidence of the interest being taken in Canadian postal achievements is found in the continuing series of visits we have by experts from other countries who come to study our service. During the past year I was pleased, as were senior officials, at the opportunity of welcoming officials from Australia, Ethiopia, the Netherlands, India, the United States and Great Britain.
I might mention that we are co-operating with the government of the West Indies federation by providing the services of a Canadian postal official to act as postal services adviser in the survey being made of the postal service systems functioning under the West Indies federation.
Because members have had before them for some months the report of my department for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1958 I will not repeat the information which it contains but I will now attempt to review for you a number of happenings and developments of the past year.
In general, the service has continued to grow at a steady pace. During the year 37 new revenue post offices were opened in rural areas and two staff post offices, two postal stations and 75 sub-post offices were opened in our larger cities. During the period from April 1, 1958 to March 31, 1959, 65 federal buildings were occupied by post offices, including our two major buildings in Winnipeg and Vancouver which contain some of the most modern postal equipment anywhere in the world.
The annual report of the Postmaster General for 1957-58 showed that our mail revenues for that year had reached a new high of $177,492,000, and that expenditures had also reached a record level of $177,893,000. During the fiscal year just completed, the one which succeeded that whose figures I have just quoted, even those record levels were surpassed as departmental revenues, revenue climbing to $183,381,000, and operating costs rose to $183,554,000. Taking the total disbursements from the total revenues you will find an excess of cost over revenues of $173,142. While it is a deficit that figure is not as large as we had presumed might be the case, and I think it reflects prudent management and careful and effective administration of the department. I might say, too, that we have succeeded in achieving this despite very substantial increases in some of the costs of our operations, and despite important improvements in our service to the public.

I should now like to speak about some of those improvements to the public. Last year, in presenting the post office estimates, I indicated that we had been concentrating on providing letter carrier service to small and medium towns which had not previously had it. We are now well on with this type of program and are increasingly turning our attention to the problem of more effective mail delivery to the sprawling suburban developments that are springing up around those large cities. Many of those new communities are separated from the nearest letter carrier areas by large tracts of undeveloped land, and hitherto they did not qualify for letter carrier service. We have decided to relax our requirements with the result that door to door service will be provided immediately to many more thousands of suburban households.
A completely new approach to the problem of providing service in scattered suburban areas is being tried through the use of a three-wheeled vehicle we call the mailmobile; my hon. friend from St. Denis calls it the scooter. Those of you who were present on parliament hill a few weeks ago when I demonstrated this versatile little machine will understand something of the high hopes we have for its use in outlying urban areas. It will enable the letter carrier to deliver not only letters but bulky mail such as parcels and newspaper bundles which now require special handling by truck. It will eliminate the need for frequent visits to relay boxes for bundles of mail deposited by truck for later pick-up and delivery by the carrier. I may say that the experiment with this new vehicle is being carried out in a suburb of Vancouver, and if successful the service will be extended to other parts of the country wherever terrain and climate permit.
In all, our carrier service during the year ended March 31, 1959 expanded with the addition of some 292 walks. Through the establishing of these walks and the revision of existing walks a total of 126,377 points of call were provided with letter carrier service. This compares with 108,036 points of call to which I referred last year when I presented my estimates. We have also taken steps to improve the service given to patrons in the fringe areas of cities and along rural routes. Requirements for group box service in suburban areas were eased, and the number of patrons required-and this will be of particular interest to our rural members -to establish a new rural route was decreased from four to three per mile. This year 865 existing routes were extended and a total of some 16,400 new patrons were brought into service along our rural routes.
Supply-Post Office
It is surprising the little things that the Post Office Department does that sometimes antagonizes the public. One of the sources of irritation to quite a few people who have spoken to me has been the lack of an official receipt requested by many patrons when they bought postage stamps in quantity at the wicket. That problem has been remedied by the development of a new receipt form we are providing to our post offices across the country so that they can provide a receipt on request to any purchaser of stamps.
Last year, to speed up service to the public, we experimented with the sale of specially packaged two and five cent stamps during the Christmas rush. That project was widely successful and we are going to improve and extend the program based on the findings of the experiment in 1958.
I have not been entirely satisfied, Mr. Chairman, with the service given our patrons under the special delivery service and we have introduced a number of modifications designed to speed up the delivery service, particularly in the larger cities. These changes, which make use of special couriers and wider use of special couriers, and less of letter carriers for special delivery mail, have speeded up this service considerably and have won general approval from postal patrons, particularly business firms.
We have been working too, to strengthen and improve our public relations division, and we hope to extend our program in this field to include a wider coverage of the smaller centres, in line with the suggestions so ably outlined last year at estimates time by the hon. member for Kootenay West. We do this because one very important aspect of our service is obtaining public co-operation, and we desire that the public shall know about what we are doing and our problems and how they themselves can work with us to obtain better mail service. We desire that as much as possible of this be done.
During the year we undertook a review of our program of annual examinations carried out for each employee of our department. I do not know how many people in this house know that postal employees, unlike most workers in many fields, are required to undergo an annual examination in the work they are doing. While the results of those examinations are not yet complete, we expect that they will determine future action with regard to our examination program which, however, in essence we feel is sound and worth while.
We have kept a close check-and the committee will be interested in this as a measure of our effectiveness-on the number of inquiries about service difficulties and investigations of irregularities, two indicators of

Supply-Post Office
potential problems within the service. I am pleased to note that inquiries have dropped from 414,332 in 1957-58 to 404,265 in 1958-59. This is a reduction of more than 10,000 over the year, and it is even more remarkable when you consider that in that same year there was a tremendous increase in the volume of mail actually handled.
In the field of security and losses, Mr. Chairman, due to continuing improvement in our methods of inspection, losses to the post office through account shortages have shown a steady decline. In the year 1957-58 there were 461 cases of shortages involving $39,184. In 1958-59 this number had dropped to 395 cases involving $22,385. These figures represent a trend which over the last two years has seen the number of cases drop by 24 per cent and the net amounts involved by 57 per cent.
We are also moving forward in our attempts to defeat break-ins and thefts from post offices. Because of improved security there was no loss in one-third of the post office break-ins last year and the average cash loss, where such occurred, has been reduced from $96 two years ago to $85 last year.
In coming to my conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say that in preparing for these estimates I reviewed my address to the house last year on the same subject. It contains much of the basic philosophy which has guided my decisions and also much additional information on this department which I will not repeat here. I mention this merely so that hon. members who may have some particular point of interest, no matter how minor it may be, which has not been covered will not feel that it has been overlooked but merely that I have tried to give them as much information as possible in a comparatively limited time. Certainly I will be delighted to explore anything anyone wants to bring up.
I should like to express a special word of appreciation to my hon. friend, the member for St. Denis, who has taken a particularly active interest in my department. While I am not sure I approve or can approve of the stockpiling of gasoline even at premium prices in Toronto for scooters that are out in Vancouver or mail delivery by Bomarc missile-
But you have advocated twice a day mail delivery.

I am
being rather pleasant at the moment and I am sorry that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has to introduce a sour note. The interest of the hon. member for St. Denis in the department, his constant concern over
(Mr. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace).]
post office matters and, I think above all, his humour and his unfailing good nature have really endeared him to me, and I want to say again how much I appreciate it.
You may be disarming him.
derive a certain satisfaction in finding pleasant people in the opposition and marking them out.
That is a very pleasant change from the situation which existed before.
Perhaps there is a more pleasant Postmaster General on this side of the house.
I am thinking of the reverse.

At
the outset of my remarks I paid a tribute to our postal employees generally and I want to emphasize again the excellent job they are doing. Because so many of us think in terms of postal employees as the ones we see, letter carriers, rural mail couriers, postmasters and those who work under them in post offices, we tend to forget that credit is due also to the administrative staff of the post office because in our department, as in all government work, administrative ability of a very high order is required.
The deputy postmaster general, our six branch heads, our regional and district directors and our area superintendents together with their staffs are all involved in this work. The great majority of them have long years of service for this is a department which must largely produce its top officials from within its own ranks, a policy with which I am firmly in accord wherever it is possible to implement it. The changes and developments we are instituting would be impossible without their co-operation and, in most cases, without their production of the actual ideas. I should like to congratulate them on the outstanding job they are doing along with our other employees.
I can speak of the post office and its operations with some feeling, for in the past two years I have become involved in its activities at all levels, from such things as the weaknesses in a stamp vending machine outside the Saint John, New Brunswick, post office, the need for name plates on the wickets at Edmonton, the leaky roof on the post office at Stephenville, Newfoundland, and the slow delivery of letter carrier shirts in Kelowna, B.C.-
And the telephone at Tecumseh.

-the
matter of a telephone in the Tecumseh post office, as the hon. member for Essex East points out; to such things as the location of major new post offices, the mechanization of mail handling processes and the introduction of the most modern electronic forms of equipment. Being always concerned beyond all else with the primary function of the department, which is to provide the best possible mail service to the Canadian public, I say without hesitation that my remarks tonight might well be summarized in the statement that the Canada post office is continually improving its service to the Canadian public and will continue that improvement in line with its very famous motto, servire populo, to serve the people.
(Translation):

On hearing the words of praise directed to me by the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) I felt that he was practically asking me to refrain from criticizing his department. Well, I don't deserve that beautiful apple green paper which has just been awarded to me. It just happens that I am in good health. And, if my questions were to the point, it was because there was ample scope for criticism.
The minister having praised me, I must necessarily return the compliment. I must say that he is a hard worker, that he is affable, likeable; he is also crafty, and intelligent.
And, above all, a Conservative.

But what I consider unfortunate is that he makes such bad use of all those fine qualities. He pays compliments. He offers the people of Canada, and hon. members in this house, all sorts of projects-but we never know whether those projects, compliments and gifts will materialize. In my college days I was taught a latin saying:
Timeo Danaos et dona Jerentes (I distrust the Greeks, even when they bring gifts.)
People with less education, perhaps, like the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard), would have said: "I distrust the Danes with their iron teeth".
You can't be beat for pettiness; you're certainly an expert at it.

When the frogs have finished croaking, we shall carry on.
Because the hon. Postmaster General as I said, is very crafty and clever, for we "knew him when", we have known him as a minister, and have also known him when he was in the opposition. Therefore the bouquets he's throwing at me now make me rather wary of what might happen if I trust his sincerity or his sweet words, be-
Supply-Post Office
cause many a minister and many a Canadian citizen have had a taste of them in the past.
When he was in the opposition, he also said complimentary things, and said what he would do if he were in office. One of my friends here reminds me of La Fontaine's fable, the one I think, about the Crow and the Fox:
SI votre ramage se rapporte a votre plumage,
Vous etes le phenix des hdtes de ces bois.
What happened was that the Postmaster General paid the compliments, but gobbled the cheese- The crow swore, but just a little too late, that he would never be taken in again. Let me say, to be kind to the hon. Postmaster General, that as far as the party in power is concerned, he is a genius. He is the prototype and the symbol of all the present cabinet. Certain ministers have certain shortcomings, others have other shortcomings, and they share the shortcomings between them; but the hon. Postmaster General has all the faults and shortcomings of all the present ministers. We must also admit that he has rare qualities: he is affable, friendly, etc., etc.; but he is a genius in the matter of promises, he is a genius in the matter of contradiction; he is a genius in the matter of confusion. He is also a genius in the matter of visions.

Two deliveries a day. (Translation):
He is a genius in nonsense.

You, you are a genius in
stupidity.

He is a genius in the matter of suggestions, suggestions of the kind that we must not forget.
He has told us about his department, the things that suited him, but left unsaid the things that were more or less to his credit. He has made a fine speech, graced with flowers of rhetoric, but he omitted all mention of the weeds concealed beneath the flowers of rhetoric that he graciously bestowed upon us.
Mr. Chairman, in order to see whether the present incumbent is a good Postmaster General, we must know of the changes that have taken place since he took over his department. We have to know if we shall close the fiscal year with a deficit or a surplus. We have to find out whether promised improvements have been carried out.
I would ask the minister not to slouch out of sight in his chair because we are going to talk a bit about his past, and his present too. As for his future, I think the people of Canada will see about it, and I am sorry for the minister, because he is a good natured,

Supply-Post Office
most affable and likeable man. It would be too bad not to see him around any more in the house and to miss his smile and his shrewdness which we highly appreciate. Unfortunately, as I just said his shrewdness is being used in a bad cause, whereas it should be serving a good one.
Mr. Chairman, I now want to say a word about the Postmaster General's estimates. The minister said nothing about them-he who, in the past, upbraided the former postmasters general for dealing with insignifiant matters, for making hollow speeches, for not comparing the Canadian Post Office Department with those of other countries, so as to show whether our own postal service was well managed. Of all this the present incumbent has spoken not a word. He merely referred to improvements that were made, or to events which took place, under departmental regulations.
Mr. Chairman, the Postmaster General can in no wise claim credit for the improvements he mentioned, because even if he had not been there, yea, even if he had vetoed them, they would have been proceeded with. Besides, the growth of those services is merely a result of a growth in the population. Those improvements existed at the time of his predecessor, and will continue to exist. However, he used to claim that such improvements could not be credited to the then minister and that if he ever got into the saddle, he would bring in drastic changes.
The improvements were made in spite of him.

Mr. Chairman, when the hon. minister was sitting on this side of the house, he used to berate us for waste and extravagance. He used to say that the Liberal party had no regard for economy, that the postal service was slow and that the experiments the government was conducting at the time were childishness and nonsense. Now, his outlook is altogether different. The things he used to call bad have now become his personal handiwork, he who was so anxious to put a stop to waste and to balance the budget.
Let us see how well he has done. Just as last year, each item of his credits shows an increase. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in the matter of extravagance, which he used to ascribe to the former government, the hon. minister now has to eat his words.
At that time, the minister used to say he was against surpluses. He would claim that the government of the time was not running things in a business-like way. In his book, business-like administration means showing deficits. In his view, bankrupt government is prosperous government. He even referred to Conservative prosperity, to past deficits
[Mr. Denis.l
and surpluses in the Post Office Department. To him, the most interesting part of the estimates is the part which concerns deficits.
How many times did he not say here that he wanted to "break even"? He was not looking for profits, but he didn't say he didn't want any deficits. The way I see it he "broke even" a little late, because since he has been running the department, there has been deficit upon deficit.
Since the minister used to advocate economy and to war against waste, there must have been waste at that time. However, his departmental estimates for this year total $163.5 million, as against $162 million last year. Such is the amount of money the minister is asking us to vote, though at the time he used to call us wastrels and spendthrifts; in 1957-58, the budget was $150 million, and in 1956-57, $132 million. Where was the waste, and where the savings, that the minister should have told us about?
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, the minister went even farther than that. In 1954, he listed the years of budget surpluses and those of budget deficits; and most years under the Liberal administration were years of surplus budgets.
He also said:

-slow moving as the department may be.

I can't understand why the various departments should not pay postage on their mailings, as does the general public.

Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) wants to write to someone, does he have to put a stamp- unattractive though it might be-on his letter? Slow moving as the department is and slow moving as the minister may be-

He was very explicit in 1954 when he said this to the minister. And he now maintains he is against surpluses. Does it mean he is in favour of deficits?
For instance, he used to lash into the minister for giving grants to Trans-Canada Air Lines. Has his department stopped paying those subsidies to the company?
Is the Postmaster General still sending mail by air? He maintains that he does. At the time he was so critical of the former government, our mail services were costing no more than $9 million, whereas today, according to the Postmaster General's report, they are costing $13 million.

a continuation of experiments made before his time. He spoke of electronic instruments; he should be honest enough to admit that those tests had begun before he was appointed to his present post. Well that is the symbol of the government, of its so-called vision, to claim all the credit for all that goes well, while anything that goes awry is blamed on the staff. And when things go wrong because of the government's own mistakes, nothing is said about it.

I thank the house, and particularly the hon. Postmaster General, for their kindness. In allowing me to complete the few remarks I had to make on this matter, I am sure the passing of the other items will be speeded up. Therefore, I shall only say a few words more.
I said a word about the civil service commission, and I shall say, in closing, that while the minister used to criticize the government for its failure to deal with the matter of salaries and working conditions, his answer now is that everything is the responsibility of the Civil Service Commission. However, if the matter of salaries is the responsibility of the Civil Service Commission today, the situation was the same at the time, and the Postmaster General knew it. However, he claimed that the then minister should intervene and that he should look after postal employees and mail carriers. But the present minister has hardly done better, because he has not even taken the trouble to attend meetings to which he has been invited.
The Postmaster General has submitted increased travel expenses, after blaming

Supply-Post Office
former ministers for allowing travel expenses to go beyond $100 thousand. Now we find that travel expenses have reached the half million dollar mark. What has happened to his sense of thrift? Where is the minister's logic? And where was the waste at the time? And what corrective measures has he applied? A little earlier, I referred to travel expenses. I think the minister must have had his share of such expenditures.
I will not ask him the amount of his travelling expenses but I feel that 25,000 or
30,000	miles to say hello to his friends in the various post offices across the country must represent a rather heavy expenditure. Even though the minister should spend 40 years visiting the various post offices, he could not tour them all; so, he just provokes emulation, rivalry and jealousy among his colleagues of the cabinet.
From now on, when complaints will be made to the department and when thousands of persons will gather to make him representations, I hope he will attend such meetings instead of presiding over a jewellers' banquet-a thing which is very important and very legitimate, I agree-but when he has to choose between two festivities, two receptions, I would suggest that he select the one which is more related to the department in his charge.
The	minister	used to	refer	to	theslowness of postal delivery. I have here a whole series of articles lambasting the present government for the sluggishness of postal	delivery.	Naturally	it is	not	the
minister's fault. However, I have here a report from a paper which I would call a "yellow paper,"-which is certainly not Liberal, because it is Montreal-Matin,-in which it is said that the special delivery service is rotten. Consequently, I do not think the minister could very well take pride in such a statement, and boast of having improved the situation.
I even have editorials referring to the same situation. The newspaper Le Soleil, which is not over friendly towards the Liberal party, stated that even during conferences, there are complaints that letters take three days to reach their destination. Our friend, Mr. Austin Cross-whom the minister knows very well-has complained that a letter posted by him had been delivered to parliament three days later.
Such occurrences were infrequent before, but in order to criticize the slowness of postal delivery, when the Liberal party was in

power, the present ministers, who were then sitting on this side of the house, used to write themselves letters and got together in attempts to put the department on the spot.
The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), who was then sitting in the opposition, used to write himself letters in 1954, to complain later on that his own letters were arriving a little late. I am convinced that the Postmaster General well remembers that.
And only recently, I was telling the hon. minister of a citizen of Montreal who complained that a letter addressed to him had reached him only six days later, while it should have been delivered to him three days before. Are we back to twice a day mail deliveries? When are we going to have twice-daily delivery in Notre Dame de Grace? Does the hon. minister recall the time when he used to claim that twice-daily deliveries would not cost more? Today, he has had a change of mind. However, he considered one-a-day delivery as absurd. Today the hon. minister says the opposite. He says people are satisfied. Why does the minister not admit that he did not have the necessary information at the time, or that he was talking through his hat? But no, we are still waiting for the twice-daily deliveries.
About publicity, the hon. minister professes to be in favour of it. Little wonder, for he has just been named the advertising man of the year. I even have his picture here; and I must say that we see it quite often in the newspapers. He has been named "the advertising man of the year". Consequently, he must not share the view of the present prime minister who used to criticize the government of the day, claiming they were spending too much on advertising.
Earlier tonight, the hon. minister dealt quite briefly with his scooters. We would like to have some information about that. Is the scooter of American manufacture? Can it be manufactured in Canada? The hon. minister knows we have unemployment in Canada. In fact, the city of Windsor, in the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), has thousands of unemployed; yet, they are experienced in that kind of work and they could very well manufacture scooters. Would it not be possible, at least to manufacture those scooters in Canada, in order to give employment to Canadians?

It would be interesting also to know the results of this experience. How many scooters have been tried? Are they left outside at night, or are they put in a garage? How many miles a gallon do you get out of them? We should be told how much they cost to operate? We should be told also if mail carriers will require a driving licence to operate those scooters.
In city, mail carriers have to carry their bags on their back, take them along wherever they go, and must not leave them unattended anywhere. When they have to walk up two or three flights of stairs, they are not allowed to let go of them. Does the same rule apply to scooter drivers or do they have to take the key up with them, and leave the scooters down in the street?
Those are questions that we would like the minister to answer ...
Mr. Chairman, those are all points on which we would appreciate a reply.

I should like to know how many stamps were issued under the present government. Judging from newspaper reports, it seems the minister is issuing two new stamps a day, instead of having two mail deliveries a day. I should like to know what representations should be made with regard to stamps. Only this morning I was reading a suggestion contained in a dispatch from Dublin, which said:

Dublin-A special postage stamp will appear here next week to commemorate the first Arthur Guiness, who 200 years ago started brewing the stout that still bears his name.

[Mr. Denis.)
villages are progressive communities and I believe that a post office, built in one or the other of those villages, would justify the expense incurred to this end.
I ask the Postmaster General to study carefully the possibility of introducing mail carrier service in the Boisjoli and Hertel districts, in the beautiful and progressive city of St. Hyacinthe. Mr. Chairman, I think the member who has just taken his seat completely missed the point of the speech made by the hon. member for St. Denis. We in this corner looked upon it as an interesting interlude in humorous pessimism and satire. Mixed with his humorous pessimism and satire were his criticisms and some of his suggestions. I must say before proceeding that we all recognize by this date in the session that the front bench of the remnants of the Liberal party-I think if I put it that way I will not get in trouble-contains a high percentage of persons with dramatic talent.
I am going to be quite parsimonious in the use of language this evening knowing the attitude of the committee and the hopes of everyone to conclude the business at as early a date as possible. I listened with great care and interest to the report made by the Postmaster General concerning his department and certain improvements in various branches. When I was listening I could not help thinking what a contrast there was between the mellow and genial exposition of the activities of the postal service of Canada by the Postmaster General this evening and the fire and brimstone that were breathed by the same person about two years ago when he was a member of the opposition. I remember that on one occasion it went on for a period of over two days. I sat very close to the hon. gentleman at that time and I could almost feel the heat on occasion.
However, regardless of the criticisms and to some extent the pessimism of the member for St. Denis, I think the post office service of Canada is a credit to the nation. It is

an enterprise in socialism that has been successful throughout the years and has been carried on not only by Progressive Conservatives but, as far as my constituency is concerned, has been carried on by people who are supporters of all parties in the house, people who are rural postmasters, rural mail couriers, postmen and so on. I think that is very splendid indeed. This service goes on night and day and when we consider the geographical extent of Canada, the physical features of our country and the many difficulties that have to be overcome compared with the provision of postal service in more densely populated countries, I think that our postal service is something to be proud of.
At this time I wish to express my appreciation of the courtesies I have received from the minister. When I write the minister letters he replies very promptly and fully and on a number of occasions he has gone into matters I have brought to his attention. I appreciate that. I think it is quite correct to say that the minister does his homework and works at his job. That is important to me. It is also true that the senior officials in Ottawa, the employees generally throughout the country, the postmasters, the rural postmasters and rural mail deliverers are a credit to the service we have in Canada at this time.
Having said that, I think we can best show our appreciation of the service rendered by the employees by giving some consideration to their representations to the government and the civil service commission for an increase in salaries. If there is one department that deserves serious consideration, the representations of the employees of the Post Office Department certainly do, the postmen who tramp the streets of the cities, villages and small towns, the rural mail carriers and postmasters in the smaller districts. In that connection I have thought for some time that serious consideration should be given to increasing the salaries of the rural postmasters. In fact, in some cases the remuneration is so unattractive that I know the department is having increasing difficulties under some circumstances in getting persons to take these positions.
With respect to the increase in salaries that has been sought by the civil service generally and by the employees of the Post Office Department, I recently read an article entitled, "Pay Boost Justified", by Mr. J. A. Norton in the C.S.A.C. Journal, March issue. I thought that Mr. Norton presented a very good case for consideration of the pay boost sought by the civil service. In the article he draws attention to the fact that the last general pay increase given to the civil service
Supply-Post Office
was in May, 1957, although there have been special increases for deputy ministers, commissioners and a few others. Since that time there has been an average increase of 9.5 per cent in the wages or salaries of employees in private industry and in some cases in provincial governments.
In addition, generally speaking the pay received by postmen, particularly the lower paid employees of the post office department, is considerably below the prevailing rates for similar services performed by persons in private industry in the districts concerned. I suggest that the employees of the post office department and the rural postmasters should receive consideration at the earliest possible time.
I want to say a word or two about postmasters over 70. I understand there is a new regulation which provides for the retirement of rural postmasters over 70. I can understand that having some general application but I do think that the regulations should provide for certain elasticity to meet special circumstances. I am quite sure that in very small places the department will find some difficulty in getting persons to replace the present postmasters. In my constituency there are a number of very estimable people who have performed this service for 30 or 40 years. There is one man to whom I might refer by way of illustration. He is a splendid old gentleman. The Postmaster General knows of the case. He is one of the few living monuments to Victorian Toryism in my constituency. He is loved by everybody. As a sentimental old revolutionary I want to say right here that I protest very much against the unfair treatment of some of these ancient Conservatives in my riding who have rendered such long and faithful service. I hope that the government will reconsider these cases, particularly where it is going to be very difficult to find someone to replace them.
I should like to say a word or two about the new post offices that are being built across the country. I think that the building of permanent, attractive, small post offices in the smaller villages and towns of Canada to a greater extent than has been carried on in the past is an excellent policy. I like the policy of the Department of Public Works, to build these post offices at a time when it will do the greatest good in relieving local unemployment. I am sure that the local people are quite willing to have the building of these post offices delayed for three, four, five or six months if it is going to serve that excellent purpose when they are being built and not have them built when there is

Supply-Post Office
plenty of activity going on in the construction field and so on. These small post offices are very much appreciated by the people in the smaller towns and villages. I have had a number of people write me about them and say they add to the local morale and pride. I hope that the government will continue this program.
I want to say a word or two about the ventilation and air conditioning in two of our larger post offices. I mentioned it on the public works estimates but I bring it to the minister's attention so that we will have the problem approached from both angles. Owing to the location of the city of Trail and the surrounding hills, which are not covered to date with a very heavy forest growth, there are at times very high temperatures in the summer months, and I think that some consideration should be given to air conditioning there during the two or three very hot summer months.
The next condition about which I complain is one from which the employees in both the Nelson and Trail post offices suffer. I was in the Nelson post office and watched the unloading of the postal bags. Lint seems to come off the bags and get into the air as a result of the handling of hundreds of bags and the ventilation in both post offices is such that the lint is not carried away by the ventilating system.
It hangs in the atmosphere above the sorting tables, shelves and bins. I told the local employees of both post offices I would bring the matter to the attention of the Postmaster General on his estimates and I have kept my word in that respect.
Now, before I conclude I do want to say a word with reference to the remarks made by the hon. member for St. Denis. He spoke with rather subtle humour, but with an element of congratulation very cleverly concealed, and said that there had been an improvement in the design of the stamps since the present Postmaster General took office. I recall that the present Postmaster General used to criticize the stamps issued by the former administration, and he was then the fire and brimstone member as far as the Post Office Department was concerned. However, I think he has done something to improve them.
If I remember correctly, during the last session he said he would enlarge the number of people with whom he would consult in this connection. I presume he has done that because I think there has been a decided improvement, and I have heard other people say that there has been a slow but progressive improvement in the design of Canadian stamps. Mind you, we have a long way

to go yet when we look at the beautiful stamps issued by some of the very small South American countries, the small South Sea islands, Borneo, and places like that. I think we have a long way to go yet, but I do think there has been improvement.
I want to refer to the stamp that the Postmaster General issued to commemorate the associated countrywomen of the world, at the suggestion of the Federated Women's Institutes of Canada. I like the idea of having co-operation with such organizations, and I suggest that approach should be continued. In this case, the women's institutes commemorative stamp committee was composed of Mrs. T. H. Howes, Mrs. James Haggerty, and Mrs. E. J. Roylance, who is a postmistress at the present time. These ladies did a very effective job in connection with the distribution of these stamps. I think this practice ought to be continued, whether it is in connection with, shall I say, occupations such as agriculture or mining or lumbering, forestry or certain trades and crafts, or whether it is commemorating a historical event that may occur at any place across this country from time to time, or historical persons. I trust the time will not be far distant when the Postmaster General will be introducing a stamp, the central figure of which will be the Mica creek dam on the Columbia river.
I like the idea of getting the co-operation of public organizations, because I am one who believes that if democracy is to function in the days ahead we have to get an increasing number of people in Canada to accept some personal responsibility and interest in all levels of government, whether it be federal or provincial. We also have to get larger numbers of people co-operating in advising on committees such as this, so that we have a greater enmeshing of those who govern with those who are being governed. This is the type of administrative twine, I should say, that will build a strong democracy.
I look forward to continued improvement in the design of stamps and, on the part of the minister, continued co-operation with various groups in Canada who by working with the department or other government organizations feel themselves to be a part of the government of Canada instead of something separate and aside. That is all I have to say at this time.

My remarks concerning the post office estimates will be brief. We all agree that post office business is big business and requires constant action on the part of the Postmaster General, his deputy, the officials in the department and all the em-

ployees in order that this improved service cannot but go on to greater things from day to day.
As a former postmaster I was very pleased to read an article which appeared in the postal Tribune, which is published in Montreal, on April 19, 1959. I am going to ask our Postmaster General if he would be good enough to read that article later on in the evening. It refers especially to some of the visits he has made. I was impressed with these remarks, as I can well remember that in my 35 years as a postmaster and supervising postmaster I never had the privilege of receiving a visit from any postmaster general until our present minister visited my office and others in my constituency. I should like to commend the Postmaster General for this most appreciated change in policy. This is a step in the right direction and his personal contact with the employees has given these civil servants the feeling that they are an important part of a great organization working for the good of the Canadian people. I hope he may continue the practice for many years.
I understand that improvements in the Post Office Department have been gradual, but there is ample evidence that all changes have been to the benefit of the service and of the employees who have been loyal in their daily duties. This loyalty is recognized by the Postmaster General and I feel certain that he will be ready to assist these fine employees with all their problems. On one of my recent trips to my constituency I was privileged to visit the Kitchener post office. This city has grown to such an extent that I found the present space in this building inadequate. In presenting this condition to the Post Office Department I suggested that a new post office should be built in the near future in order that the postmaster and his staff could continue the same excellent service that has been provided in the past. My recommendation is being investigated by the department, and I do appreciate the fine cooperation that has been extended to me in regard to this urgent matter.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Chairman, as a former employee, I should like to extend the appreciation of all employees to the Canadian postmasters association and its affiliates in each of the provinces. These associations have done splendid work and are grateful to the Post Office Department for their kind assistance and co-operation.

As to their postal duties, they are responsible to the Postmaster General in Ottawa, and with regard to their telegraphic duties they were responsible to the superintendent of Canadian National Telegraphs. and to revise the policy so that post office buildings will be provided on the basis of need and not on the basis of revenue or on the basis of a building having existed prior to confederation.
