speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to hold up my own estimates, but might we revert for a brief period to item 303?

Agreed.
303. Preparatory work, not within the fields of particular departments, on emergency defence measures, $175,000.

Perhaps I may be allowed to deal with this matter at this point. I appreciate very much the attitude taken by the committee. This is, however, a matter to which some reference must be made at this time, namely the emergency organization. As I stated on the last occasion on which the estimates were before this committee and, later on, on two occasions, it is necessary now to prepare in advance the measures which would have to be taken if a major war were to commence suddenly in all the fury of a nuclear onslaught. I have already set out something with regard to the emergency organization which has been established, and given details in connection therewith. However, in the last few months further planning and organization has taken

place to preserve some degree of governmental and economic organization and continuity throughout the initial period of a nuclear war. The purpose we have had in mind has been to decentralize as far as possible.
I do not propose to review what I said on March 23 in that connection as to the course to be taken to provide for the continuance of government and governmental activities in the event of war. The whole problem was discussed in detail on April 24 by several of my colleagues with ministers representing the provinces.
On May 28 an order in council was passed under the Public Service Re-arrangement and Transfer of Duties Act, redistributing civil defence functions, some to national defence, some to national health and welfare, some to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and some to the emergency measures organization of the privy council office. These changes will go into effect on September 1 and the various groups concerned are now making ready to undertake their several responsibilities in this field. The main purpose of the changes in distribution of civil defence duties has been to closely integrate them with the general government organization for war purposes.
My purpose in rising is to announce a decision which the cabinet has made within the last three days relating to wartime organization. As hon. gentlemen opposite who were members of the former government realize, general plans in this connection were considered by the former government and those plans have been considered and advanced in the last two years. Direction has been given to the Department of Defence Production to plan now in peacetime a war supplies agency to be established immediately on the outbreak of war. This agency would have full responsibility and authority for all aspects of control over the production, distribution and pricing of both civil and military supplies other than production on farms and the catching and landing of fish, during the early part of a nuclear war, at least.
Study of the probable economic situation arising from conditions of nuclear attack indicates that the problem of providing and distributing essential commodities for both military and civilian purposes would be critical and complicated. Decisions would have to be taken promptly and any doubt as to where authority lay could result in serious delay and confusion. It would be necessary to have not only an organization with clear, unified control over supplies of all types, but one that could be decentralized not only to regional, but if necessary to local areas.
Supply-Privy Council
Those who recall the organization in the last war might visualize the agency as combining most of the responsibilities of the department of munitions and supply and of the wartime prices and trade board. The problems of allocation and distribution in the beginnings of a nuclear war would be vital. As time goes on, should the war continue, we would expect to see circumstances change considerably and it might then be desirable to vary the type of organization now proposed.
It has been decided that the necessary preparations for establishing this agency should be put in the hands of a single unit with assistance from others as required. A review of the functions and responsibilities of the several departments in legislation and in practice led to the conclusion that the Department of Defence Production would be the most suitable one to undertake this task, but requiring the assistance of the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture.
It will be noted that the establishment of this new agency will change somewhat the distribution between departments of wartime duties and the preparations for them which I outlined to the house last year. The war supplies agency will require a considerable regional and local organization ready to swing into action on short notice. We would expect it to utilize the field staff of government departments that are qualified to assist it in emergency such, for example, as the numerous officers of the Department of Agriculture in meeting the demand of food supplies.
The agency will require the help of many people throughout the country if it is to be ready for a wartime emergency. In due course we shall therefore have to call for the voluntary service of many competent executives, both from private and public life, to prepare themselves to assume responsibilities on short notice should war occur. We shall also have to obtain for the use of this organization the fullest information on local supplies, facilities and requirements.
Another area which will demand detailed attention in the near future is that of preparations to make the most effective use of motor transport under conditions of nuclear war. The officials are being asked to initiate discussions of this subject both with provincial authorities and with representatives of those engaged in the motor transport industry. In the uncertain and inevitably confused conditions to be expected as a result of nuclear attack it is considered that the flexibility and widespread distribution of motor

Supply-Privy Council transport facilities would be of major importance in helping Canadians to survive and reorganize the economy.
I am able to inform the committee-and I think it is important that the committee should know this-that we now have ready facilities from which a central core of the dominion government can carry on outside of Ottawa under conditions of nuclear war, even if there is serious radioactive fallout in this area. Emergency communications facilities have been or are being established to be used if the regular channels of communications are interrupted. We propose to amplify and improve these emergency communications facilities, for such communications will be of vital importance in maintaining the country as a going concern.
We are now in the course of planning the arrangements for emergency regional centres from which the various federal organizations will be able to operate in each province under war conditions, and tie in with both the provincial and military authorities in the area. The local arrangements will have to be reviewed in considerable detail with each of the provinces as soon as that is possible, relating them to the needs and plans of the various agencies concerned as these are developed.
The main expenditures involved in these arrangements are not covered in this Privy Council office vote but under the appropriations of the other departments co-operating in these general matters.
To what vote is the Prime Minister referring?

Vote No. 303, Mr. Chairman.
These are closely related to the regular duties of those departments and it seems best to leave them there for reasons of security. I point that circumstance out and underline it. In the various departments, naturally, there will not be full detail as to the measures taken but only the general outline being given by myself on this question.
The staff and expenses of the small central unit in the Privy Council office which this vote is intended to cover will have to be increased to carry the larger load involved by the transfer of civil defence duties. For this year, these increased costs will be borne by transfers of funds from the civil defence vote in accordance with the practice when duties are transferred under the Public Service Re-arrangement and Transfer of Duties Act. The increase in staff shown in the figures in the blue book on page 403 covers the five regional officers that have been appointed. Offices are now being opened in Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and


Vancouver. As soon as possible five more will be opened so that we will have one in each province. This has been made necessary by the burden of work that will arise out of the new civil defence duties.
In placing this plan before the committee in some detail I want to emphasize that the taking of this course of action is not in any way to be construed as evidence of any increase in international tension or added fears in recent months, but simply as a course of action in which care and caution must be exercised by those with responsibilities to the end that should nuclear war take place the necessary preparations would have been made to assure the continuance of the government and to maintain Canada in a position of strength and stability. I want to make that abundantly clear because some might interpret what I said as indicative of a greater fear as to the immediate future internationally and I want to underline that. That is not the reason for this very extensive plan to assure the maintenance of government and security should nuclear war take place.

Mr. Chairman, it is, of course, wise and well that government should take precautionary plans of this kind. I think at the same time the Prime Minister was well advised to emphasize that the announcement of the advancement of those plans now does not mean in any way, shape or form that the contingency which they are designed to meet is any closer than it was a year ago. Indeed, perhaps we may hope-there does not always seem to be very much ground for hope, but we must hope-that that contingency will recede. Nevertheless, any government has an obligation of this kind to plan and it is satisfactory to know that the government is discharging that obligation.
The Prime Minister in his announcement, however, dealt with a very important subject, the subject of emergency powers, the basis for such emergency powers and the circumstances under which those emergency powers might come into effect. I am going to ask the Prime Minister whether he would let this particular item stand until tomorrow so that we can have an opportunity to study the statement which he made tonight? I can assure him we do not do this with any desire to hold up the estimates but it is such an important statement that perhaps he would give us the opportunity to study it. I want to endorse the

Mr. Chairman, I, too, of course, am quite in accord with the suggestions that have been made. I think I can answer that at once, even though I am going entirely to accede to the request as particularly amplified by the member for Essex East. In the
Supply-Privy Council event that war should come, then immediately reliance would be placed on the terms of the War Measures Act and the extraordinary powers therein provided would immediately become applicable.

Now, with respect to the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition and amplified and given greater particularity by the member for Essex East, may I say this. 67. Salaries and contingencies of the commission, $3,661,089.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a brief comment on this item regarding the civil service and the employment of any person by any branch or any department of the government service anywhere in Canada. We are constantly reminded of unemployment in this country. The civil service of Canada is the largest employer of labour in Canada. The unemployed in Canada are in the main men under the age of 50 years with the responsibilities of men of that age group.
Civil service regulations demand that preference for employment be given to Canada's veterans. Surely this preference should also be maintained in other branches of the government not under regulations governing the civil service and particularly in the service of the House of Commons itself.
In addition, civil service regulations set the statutory age of retirement at 65. With some unemployment in Canada, with many men well below the age of 65 unemployed, surely the public service of Canada should be the first to set an example to employers and should retire employees over the age of 65 to make way for entry into the service of Canada of these younger men now unemployed. The argument may be used that only certain men and women are retained beyond this age because of knowledge and experience but, this argument is not valid when it is used to break a statutory provision affecting the public service of Canada. No man or woman is irreplaceable and I strongly urge on the government that it should fulfil the self-imposed obligation of retirement of its employees at 65 and so ease the present burden of unemployment.

Mr. Chairman, before asking the house to consider the estimates of the civil service commission I should like to present the new chairman of the civil service commission, Mr. Samuel Hughes, Q.C., formerly a judge of the Supreme Court of Ontario. He has assumed a very important

responsibility. An effective, independent civil service commission is, in many respects, the key to an efficient public service. The civil service commission may become even more important in the near future. As you know, the government expects to introduce legislation at the next session which may have a significant bearing on the commission in particular and the public service in general.
The government was pleased, therefore, to be able to appoint to the post of chairman a man with so many qualifications and proven capacity in so many fields. Mr. Hughes has a bachelor of arts degree from the university of Toronto and a master of arts degree from Oxford university, and is a member of the Ontario bar. He has had wide experience as a teacher, lawyer, judge, administrator and military officer. His legal training will be a special asset when the Civil Service Act goes before parliament for review. Fortunately, he is also a young man who should be able to cope for many years to come with his numerous responsibilities. I am sure the house will join with me in wishing him well.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the absence of the Leader of the Opposition I think I should perhaps say a word in connection with what the Secretary of State has just said. I would not for a moment want what I am about to say to be considered as disrespectful in the slightest degree. I have been a member of the house now for a great many years and this is the first time that I have heard a statement such as that just made by the Secretary of State. Civil servants, no matter how high an office they hold and how respectful they are, are anonymous and have been so in the House of Commons.
Having said that, I repeat that I would not want the gentleman to whom the minister has referred in such eulogistic terms to believe that we on this side of the house do not hesitate to hope that he will fulfil the office to which he has been appointed in the manner in which such offices are generally fulfilled in the civil service of Canada. But I did think, I should bring to the attention of the house the rather unusual procedure of the minister which I hope, in the future, will not be followed as a precedent. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, in spite of the restrictions just now suggested by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), may I also be allowed to congratulate the new chairman. I hope he will continue the good work of his predecessors. I also want to congratulate the two other members of the commission, Miss Addison and Mr. Pelletier for the considerable amount of work they have taken upon themselves since the de-
Supply-Secretary of State parture of the former chairman who went back to his diplomatic career. They appeared before the committee and proved themselves equal to the situation. They certainly deserve to be warmly commended.
The civil service of Canada is an organization which, since its very beginning, certainly has been very deserving. It has rendered great services, but there are some things which might be improved; indeed, the commission has often asked for those improvements.
I have here the annual report of the civil service commission for the year 1958. This is what it says on page 6:
Personnel selection
It has been difficult to supply government hospitals with all the required staff. There is, in particular, a lack of nurses, physiotherapists, rehabilitation therapists and laboratory technicians. There is also a lack of ship inspectors for the Department of Transport. After having satisfied itself that Canadian resources in that field were about exhausted, the commission made some offers of employment in the United Kingdom, which have led to a number of appointments.
And further on, on the same page we see the following:
At higher levels than that of admission, it has been difficult to find good candidates among science graduates who left university a few years ago. Quite naturally, a good number of the best university graduates have interesting positions in other fields, so that a real problem obtained when the commission had to fill the needs of the various departments.
And, on page 7, we find the following paragraph:
For instance, it has been impossible for some time to find enough graduates specialized in mathematics, physics or physical engineering and who could become meteorologists, nor a sufficient number of commerce graduates who might become income tax assessors. The problem is due to the fact that the number of graduates in those fields is comparatively small, whereas demand, by government services as well as private industry, remains high.
Well, Mr. Chairman, there is a reason for such conditions and it is an absolutely simple one. They are due to the fact that salaries offered in the civil service for such positions are entirely inadequate.
Accountants were required and, on many occasions, I sent out those forms we get from the civil service commission to all the accountants I know. Not one of them wanted any of those positions, because the salaries they get in private industry are much higher than those offered by the civil service com-sission. I am not blaming the civil service commission, since it cannot fix the salaries; that has to be done by the government, and the civil service commission has but to comply with government orders in that respect.

Supply-Secretary of State
This morning I received posters asking for information officers. Let us have a look at the qualifications required:
High school degree, additional credits for further academic training.
Several years' experience in publicity work.
Good knowledge of publicity media and methods.
Ability to draft and prepare, for publication, publicity texts, etc.
And for that, a salary of $5,700 to $6,180, is being offered, when it is known that in private industry, those people earn $7,000 to start with, and can obtain higher salaries later. How can you expect them to leave a $7,000, $8,000 or $9,000 job to accept one at $5,700?
I have here a poster asking for technical officers, at a salary ranging from $3,420 to $4,020; the required qualifications are as follows:
Degree from a recognized university or good general education, acquired after good and adequate training or experience, and a good many years of experience in the field of public relations.
Demonstrated ability to perform the duties involved in the field of external relations.
Personal suitability; satisfactory physical condition, etc.
For all this, we offer to a university graduate a salary ranging from $3,420 to $4,020. Is it reasonable to think that a university graduate who could get a much higher salary in private industry would accept to sacrifice his life to work for the public service?
And further on, we ask for lawyers. The salary that is offered is $4,740. If a lawyer is not worth more than that, he does not deserve to be a member of the Bar.
It is for those reasons that the government cannot get lawyers, because they all earn more than that, especially during these years when money has lost its value and when people have a good deal of it to spend.
Then, we ask for economics or commerce graduates from a Canadian university. How much do we offer them? Imagine! $4,560 a year! It is utterly ridiculous. How can we expect people who have made serious studies, who have followed a classical course for eight years, or a university course of three, four or five years, to accept to work for such low salaries.
Well, I cannot understand it. One of these days, the government will have to decide to revise the salaries which continue to dwindle, because of the cost of living continuing to rise. As I said earlier, those salaries are ridiculously low for professionals who have made serious studies. Well, as long as those


salaries are not increased, it will be difficult for the commission to find civil servants.
In that field, as I was saying, the civil service commission has no jurisdiction, because the money is voted by the government or rather by parliament at the government's request. Now, the Civil Service Commission is asking for it. The government has received the civil service commission's report dealing with salary increases. Now we ask the minister what he proposes to do, and his reply is that "we are not ready". After two years of consideration the minister tells us: "We are not ready to act, and we must still discuss the matter."
Mr. Chairman, as long as discussions go on and no action is taken, I am sure the civil service commission despite all its efforts, and despite the high calibre of its commissioners and of the new chairman, will be unable to recruit the required staff.
While providing an appropriate salary for professional people, one must not be unmindful especially of the small civil servant, the one who earns hardly $2,000 or $3,000 a year, who, like the others, has a family to feed and children to educate. In my opinion, the civil servant is in a worse predicament, because the government is taking no action in the matter.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the Secretary of State to be kind enough to use his authority, if he has any and I hope he has-they are not all members for Three Rivers in the cabinet-I hope, as I said, that he will use his authority to urge the other cabinet ministers to take action in favour of the lower paid employees who are in need.
I know people who have a hard time making both ends meet and who are obliged to reduce their standard of living substantially in the way of clothing and food. These civil servants are obliged to come to Ottawa to work. They are not satisfied with the clothes they wear, but they cannot afford to buy any other because their wages are insufficient, due to the increase in the cost of clothing and food.
We have read in the French newspapers as well as in the English ones, the dissatisfaction expressed by the federal civil servants. In fact, here is what Le Droit of July 16, had to say about it:
Civil servants dissatisfied with all those delays.
The National Joint Council of Canada has expressed to the Hon. Donald Fleming its dissatisfaction regarding the delays of the government to accept the civil service commission's recommendations about the salaries of the civil servants.

The council, 120,000 member strong, would like to know the reasons for these delays and has asked Mr. Fleming for a meeting. The letter answered that he could not set a time for a meeting because, due to the late stage of the session, he was overworked.
It follows then that the civil servants are running the risk of seeing the matter postponed until the next session.
Mr. Fleming said in the house that the government and the civil service commission had to study this matter further before the recommendations of the commission could be taken as final.
Mr. Chairman, we understand the dissatisfaction of the civil servants. But what we, on this side, do not understand is that after a two year study of this report of the civil service commission, which had also produced interim reports, it is, I repeat, that after studying a complete report for two years, this government cannot see its way clear to examining it in order to give justice to those who need it.
I know very well that the Secretary of State is going to say that his job is only to submit the estimates of the civil service commission to parliament and that he has nothing to do with an independent Commission. I am not asking him to interfere in the administration of the civil service commission or to tell the commissioners: "You will do this or that". I am just asking him to use his authority-and I hope he has some-to urge the Minister of Finance, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and all his colleagues of the government so that they may decide at last to do something in order that we should have something positive in that field.
Mr. Chairman, I find also that mention was made of an independent outside commission which would be required to inquire into the civil service commission. I am definitely against such a suggestion. I know that we have here the agencies capable of doing that job and I submit that we do not have to go out to find so-called efficiency experts who have failed pitifully wherever they went. They would probably prove a failure in the civil service commission as elsewhere. We have the experts we need. The civil service commission has conducted a serious study of the whole situation. The only thing it needs to act and to carry out its plans is additional staff. With its present staff, the civil service commission is unable, in some departments, to carry out direct supervision of departmental promotion competitions. That is why I ask the Secretary of State to
Supply-Secretary of State kindly give in to the civil service commission, so that the commission may better do its job for the government.
(Text):

The civil service of Canada, as I think all hon. members will agree, has enjoyed an extremely high reputation over the past number of years. A considerable part of the credit for that high reputation must, I think, properly go to the civil service commission for their competence and impartiality in selecting persons to fill the vacant positions. I can only express the wish that that credit can continue to go to the comission over the years that lie ahead of us. I perhaps do not need to elaborate on that subject unduly here tonight. However, it is of the utmost importance in the administration of the country's business that the commission or the hiring agent of government preserve its competent method of hiring and, above all, its impartiality in hiring.
Therefore, as the new chairman of the commission takes over his duties, I want to express the hope that this record of impartiality is continued in the future. There are some persons who are greatly concerned on this subject and there are bits and pieces of evidence that support their concern. However, I do not need to elaborate on that matter either, other than to warn the government that if the minister, in the legislation which he forecasts for the next session of parliament, in the changes in the civil service act and in the other legislation concerning the public service, does anything that would in any way weaken the position that has been built up over the years of administering promotions and the selection of civil servants on an impartial basis, he will have done a great disservice to his own government and to the country at large. I want to leave that note of warning to him on record so that, as he considers the legislation proposed for introduction at the next session of parliament, he will have it in mind.
There is one particular matter that I want to raise, and I think I can deal with it briefly. It is this, and I would ask the minister to make a note of it. In connection with a position of caretaker, grade 5, at Brantford, Ontario, competition number 59-J-685, the competition was held in the ordinary way by the commission. The results of the competition were published in the Canada Gazette of July 11, 1959 at page 2460. The winner of the competition was notified in the ordinary way of his appointment to the position and he took over his

Supply-Secretary of State *duties in the position. Incidentally, I may say that the position carries with it certain housing accommodation. He purchased certain equipment for the housing quarters, moved in and so on. Then after occupying the position for a short time he was moved out of it and the man who came third in the competition was placed in the position.
Those are the facts as I have them. I want to add only one other detail. The man who came first in the position-and I hope the hon. member for Wetaskiwin will bear this in mind because I want to support part of his remarks on this point-is a man entitled to the veterans overseas preference. The man who came third did not have any overseas preference. In the filling of that position something happened that is not in accordance with the civil service procedure as laid down by the civil service commission. There appears to be some irregularity that should be looked into immediately and corrected. In addition to that irregularity of the man who came first in the competition not getting the position or being moved out of it after he had moved from his former position at considerable expense to himself, he incurred a financial loss, because of the nature of the position, in having to buy certain equipment. I do not expect the Secretary of State to have the details of these positions here in order to discuss them on these estimates but I would ask him to undertake to have that matter examined thoroughly, to see that justice is done and to see that the regulations of the commission are adhered to and that correct procedure is followed in all respects in that matter.

I rise on this item to say again, as I said last session, that I think the term civil servant is a rather degrading one to apply to people who are employed by the government of Canada. I, personally, would like to see some other title applied to them, rather than the one which is used now. However, I understand that the minister does not agree with that approach or, at least, he did not last session. He thought that the term "civil servant" degrading as it is was good enough for the people who are working in the public employ.
I listened with interest to the impassioned remarks of the hon. member for Hull with respect to salary adjustments and the salary scale of people in the employ of the government of Canada. I think this government and the government which preceded it have been tackling this question from the wrong end. I think a much more sensible arrangement would be to treat the employees of the government in a manner different from that in which they are treated at present. In other words,


they should not be treated as people in a class not quite the same as other employees in the country. They should not, in fact, be treated as second class citizens when it comes to wages, hours and working conditions. Instead, they should be placed on precisely the same basis as other workers and treated in the same way as we expect other employers in Canada to treat their staffs, though, of course, I do not suggest that exactly the same machinery need be used for reaching conclusions on wages, conditions, and hours of work. I do suggest, however, that these employees should be treated in the same way as employees of the C.N.R., Trans-Canada Air Lines, or any other of the crown corporations which report to parliament through various ministers.
I believe that if a group of employees decides to get together and form a bargaining unit, as has been done in a number of cases or, probably in all cases, I think that organization should have the right to ask its employer-the federal government-to sit down and bargain with it in good faith. This cap in hand attitude, this pleading with the government for favourable consideration of improvements in wages, hours and working conditions should become a thing of the past. Now it is only too easy for the Minister of Finance or some other minister to put them off for reasons which, in my opinion, are not adequate. I believe that the federal government should be prepared to sit down and bargain over working conditions and so on just as other employers are bound to do. As it is, government employees have to wait expectantly hoping for the benevolence of the government to reach such proportions that an increase is granted. I do not think that should be our attitude in so far as the wage and salary structure of civil servants is concerned.
We would be far better off if they had bargaining rights and established arrangements under which they, like other employees in Canada who are represented by a union or an agency could sit down and discuss the question of wage increases, wage adjustments, hours of work and all the other things over which unions bargain. I do not think that these employees in the public service want the right to strike as do other employees working for other employers. I do not think they would be agreeable to go that far. But we should, I think, provide some machinery which would make it possible to reach a conclusive agreement in so far as their wages, hours and working conditions are concerned.
If such an agreement cannot be reached directly with the federal government, they should have the right to proceed to an outside

tribunal or to an arbitration board to settle these problems in precisely the same way as do the firefighters who work for municipalities. These firefighters do not have the right to strike. In fact many years ago they wrote into their constitution that they should not, because they felt that their work was of such importance to the community that they did not believe they should even think in terms of withholding their services. But this example shows that there is a group of employees, working for municipalities in many cases, which has the right to proceed to arbitration, if necessary, to settle any differences as to wages and conditions which may arise with their employers and this, I suggest, is the attitude which the federal government should take as far as its employees are concerned.
May I say this to the committee. Let the government cease participating any further in this patronizing attitude towards its employees in the public service. Let it place them on the same level as the employees of other organizations, whether crown companies or public companies, and let them be given the right which is justly theirs to make a collective determination as far as negotiations are concerned instead of treating them as being second class citizens, because they are not.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like for one moment to re-echo the views expressed here by the hon. member for Ottawa West. I think it is vital that the minister should realize the significance of impartiality in the civil service commission. No one I am sure is more conversant with the situation than the minister himself and I am sure that no one would want a situation of impartiality to obtain more so than does the Prime Minister himself.
Over the years that I have been in the house there have been many chairmen of the civil service commission, beginning, first of all, when I arrived here in 1935, with Mr. C. H. Bland, who for many years occupied that position, and occupied it with distinction. He was a man who was not only devoted to the position which he held, but one who succeeded in instituting in the civil service commission many improvements and innovations.
He was there for many years and I think that representatives of both sides of this house would vouch for the fact that he fulfilled his duties with efficiency and distinction. I think that applies, also, to the man who succeeded him, though for a short period of time -Mr. Nelson. It certainly could be said of the last man who occupied the post prior to the appointment of Mr. Justice Hughes, and I speak, of course, of Ambassador Heeney. The
Supply-Secretary of State fact that he was appointed by the former government and retained by this government indicates, I believe, the confidence which both administrations had in the man who had held that high office. I have not the slightest doubt that the incumbent of the office at present will wish to follow in the footsteps of these three distinguished civil servants.
It seems to me that the attention of the minister and the committee should be directed again to the points which the hon. member for Ottawa West made. It is of extreme importance to the country, to the government and to the civil service commission that there should be in that great and important body impartiality so that there be selected for the service of the government the best candidates that are available.
(Translation):
Just one question, Mr. Chairman, to ask the minister whether the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson), who is now sitting by his side, has been appointed his parliamentary secretary?

I am sure the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) does not expect an affirmative answer.

Public Printing and Stationery-
311. Department administration, $656,595. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, we shall now deal with the national printing bureau. If you will allow me, I should like, first of all, to read a few pages from the Senate and House of Commons Act, Revised Statues, 1952, chapter 249. Section 15 reads as follows:
No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with any other, by himself or by the interposition of any trustee or third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing any contract or agreement, expressed or implied, with or for the government of Canada on behalf of the crown, or with or for any of the officers of the government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is to be paid, is eligible as a member of the House of Commons, or shall sit or vote in the said House.
And the last eight lines of section 16, read as follows:
... or performs any service for the government of Canada, or for any of the officers of the government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is paid or to be paid, whether such contract, agreement or sale is expressed or implied, and whether the transaction is single or continuous, the seat of such member shall thereby be vacated, and his election shall thenceforth be null and void.
And section 19 reads as follows:
(1) In every contract, agreement or commission to be made, entered into or accepted by any person with the government of Canada, or any of the departments or officers of the government of

Supply-Secretary of State Canada, there shall he inserted an express condition, that no member of the House of Commons shall be admitted to any share or part of such contract, agreement or commissions, or to any benefit to arise therefrom.
(2) In case any person, who has entered into or accepted, or who shall enter into or accept any such contract, agreement or commission, admits any member or members of the House of Commons, to any part or share thereof, or to receive any benefit thereby, every such person shall, for every such offence, forfeit and pay the sum of two thousand dollars, recoverable with costs in any court of competent jurisdiction by any person who sues for the same.
And section 20 says:
This Act does not extend to disqualify any person as a member of the House of Commons by reason of his being
(a) a shareholder in any incorporated company.
There is just a mention of a shareholder. I have quoted that section not to make any accusation, but to ask the minister to investigate a case which seems to me quite extraordinary. I find, in the answers given to questions I asked, that the Monitor Publishing Company of Montreal was awarded four contracts, one for $10,416, another for $255, a third one for $128 and the last one for $128, for a grand total of $10,922. And I was told,-which seems to be confirmed,-that a member of the board of directors of the Monitor Publishing Company of Montreal is the member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken). If that is clearly established, I am not judging anything nor making any direct accusation, but I want things to be cleared up.
This is what the law says:
This Act does not extend to disqualify any person as a member of the House of Commons by reason of his being
(a) a shareholder in any incorporated company.
Mention is not made anywhere of a director or a president or a member of the management of a company. It was then the intent of the legislator to exclude only the shareholder who generally has his say only once a year at the general meeting while the director, a lady director, a president of a vice president are continually looking after the business of the company and are directing its policy.
Thus the director, president or vice president of a company is so much closer to the administration and his position is a lot more advantageous than that of the shareholder. Therefore I urge the minister to consider making an inquiry in that with a view to finding if what happened in the case of the member for York-Humber places her definitely in the situation of a member who cannot sit in this house for having a contract with the government or for having


been involved in it directly or indirectly when that Montreal publishing company got contracts for $10,922 during the year. If the act is not sufficiently clear to necessitate definitely the re-election of the member, then I say that the time has come for the government to undertake a revision of that Senate and House of Commons act in order to clarify the situation. This might be the first occurrence of such a case; it might be that the member for York-Humber does not know about that section, she might be acting in good faith, but it is very dangerous for a member to be a director in a company dealing with the government.
Therefore I urge the hon. minister to make an extensive inquiry because this is a serious case. I am not laying any charge, but the situation ought to be clarified as much in the interest of the member for York-Humber as of all the other members in this house. It is important that people know what are the duties, obligations and privileges of members, arising out of their election to the House of Commons.
Now I find here, on page 19, that a certain Mont-Laurier firm, namely Le Flambeau, has received an amount of $2,019.75 under a contract. This firm, I am informed, was started on February 24, 1959, and according to the court records, Le Flambeau is registered under the ownership of a Mr. Paquette. It is even claimed-I have no proof, but I am merely reporting what is commonly said on the street-
The House of Commons is no place for jokes.

Now I should like to know whether that is a fact. speechtext: Yes; I can give the Schell case as one; another case was the Boothby case in the United Kingdom which I put on the record and three or four others which leave my mind at the moment; but the circumstances and the procedure were quite clearly laid down and I submit to you with deference that the hon. member is within the rules in proceeding as he has.

On
the point of order-

Legalized slander.

You are also a backbencher; what are you talking about?

(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I would like to kill those rumours and say immediately to the hon. member for Hull that since 1945, Mr. Gilbert Paquette owns a newspaper called Le Flambeau, I do not believe there is a Mr. Lesage or any other person associated with him, except that an old printer who worked in another printing plant in Mont-Laurier has gone into business with him.

I fully accept the explanation of the minister, and to prove that I accept them quite well, I leave the matter at that.
Mr. Chairman, there is another rather delicate matter, with which I want to deal and for which I do not blame the minister directly. I know that the minister cannot supervise by himself 25,000, 30,000 or 35,000 contracts which are granted annually.
I know that the minister does not have, in the Printing Bureau division, the necessary staff which could help him as it should be. I know that the minister should have had for a long time a Queen's Printer who is, after all, his deputy minister. It is unfortunate for the minister that this appointment has not been made, since the situation I am referring to might not have occurred.
I asked a question regarding the binders, and I notice among the answers I was given and bearing the minister's signature, that in some cases there were three bidders. Wilson Jones Limited, E. G. Thomas & Son, Cope-land-Chatterson Ltd. Wilson Jones' bid was for $5,516, E. G. Thomas & Son's was for $5,900, and that of Copeland-Chatterson Ltd. was for $8,910. And in that particular

Supply-Secretary of State case, it was the highest bidder, Copeland-Chatterson Ltd., with $8,910 who got the contract.
In the second case, there were five bidders: Wilson Jones Limited, Toronto, $5,590; E. G. Thomas & Son Ltd., $6,260; Brown Bros. Ltd., Toronto, $6,370, Copeland-Chatterson Ltd., from Brampton, $8,910, and Chas. Chapman Co. Ltd., from London, $8,090. The contract was again awarded to the highest bidder who was Copeland-Chatterson Ltd., from Brampton, for $8,910.
In the third case, which is different from the others, there were only two bidders: Wilson Jones Limited, $13,680, and Copeland-Chatterson Ltd., $17,820. In that case, the contract was awarded to the lowest bidder, which was Wilson Jones, for an amount of $13,680.
As far as the fourth case is concerned, there were two bidders; Wilson Jones Limited, $7,040, and Copeland-Chatterson Ltd., $7,840. In this case the contract was awarded to the hihest bidder, that is to Copeland-Chatterson Ltd., for an amount of $7,840.
And we have the fifth case where there is only one bidder, and where only one bid was made, that of Copeland-Chatterson Ltd., for an amount of $21,330.
I admit that following this information, there is an explanatory letter which says among other things-and if I am wrong in my explanation I wish to be corrected-that Copeland and Chatterson Ltd. is mode competent than other firms for the type of binders requested by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. However, I read this on page 3:
(Text):
A requisition dated May X, 1959 for 2,000 binders was received. Copeland-Chatterson was asked to quote for 2,000 English and 1,000 French. Prices of Copeland-Chatterson, $21,330 ($7.11 each).
On June 3, a submission was made to treasury board which requested that authority be given to enter into contract with Copeland-Chatterson. The remarks on the submission were as follows:
"Tenders were not invited from other firms in this case as our experience indicates that no other firm has been able to demonstrate that they can meet the exact specifications."
(Translation) :
As you see, Mr. Chairman, the explanation is given that Copeland-Chatterson Ltd. were the only firm qualified to do this work. However, in one of these tenders, the contract was awarded to the lowest bidder, namely Wilson Jones Limited. Therefore there is certainly something which is definitely not justifiable, and I am wondering how they went about to determine the qualifications of the others, or their lack of qualifications,


of whether they just relied on Copeland-Chatterson Ltd. to establish what they wanted.
I believe that the other firms should have been given the same opportunity of carrying out this project. I understand that the request had been made by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, and that tenders had been called by the printing and stationery division. Well, I submit that if we had given the other firms the same opportunity of going ahead and building binders, it would certainly have been possible to find the means to enable them to make something comparable to the work performed by Copeland-Chatterson Ltd.
I wonder if that question should not be submitted to the public accounts committee next year, so that we might hear the representatives of those other firms, that is Wilson Jones Limited, E. G. Thomas & Son Ltd., Brown Bros. Ltd. and Chas. Chapman Co. Ltd. They might explain their side of the story and we could ask them to produce the samples submitted by those companies, in order to see whether the difference was such to justify, when submissions were asked for in every case except one, awarding the contract to the highest tenderer.
I ask the Secretary of State to see to it that this situation be examined by the public accounts committee next year, so that we may get this thing cleared off and see if it was really impossible to do otherwise.
Mr. Chairman, I said it was easy to find objections, particularly where senior officials of a department are concerned. However, as I said a moment ago, I would not like to lay the blame directly on the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, (Mr. Comtois). However, we might perhaps lay the blame, to some extent, on some officials who are responsible for the distribution. As I say, it is easy to raise objections when it is a case of proving that a firm is better than another, especially when it is perhaps inferior to the first one, and that simply because it does not please a particular official of some department.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I would ask that the matter be referred to the public accounts committee, next year, in order that the minister, as well as we, may be quite clear on that. He would also be in a better position than he is tonight to give us an answer, because he has with him just an explanatory letter, which was not written by himself, but

which he received from his under-secretary or some other official, without having had time to examine it carefully.
If the committee were asked to look into that matter, it would enable us to get information from the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys in order to ascertain for whom that work has been done. I appreciate that he is not in a position to give us an answer, because it is the officials of the printing bureau who, in letting the contract, have asked in this way.
I want to know if it would be possible to establish that the contract could have been given to the lowest bidder. In doing so, the government would have paid less, and at the same time the system of this division of the printing bureau would have been kept impeccable, as it has been done rather frequently in the past.
(Text):

I have one question to put to the minister. He will remember that last year he gave the assurance that his officials were going to try their best to spread these printing contracts beyond the Ontario-Quebec triangle. I should like him to give us an indication how this spread has been effected in the last financial year by giving some figures that will show how many more contracts have gone to the western provinces and the eastern provinces than in the year before in terms of their value. How successful has the minister been in spreading these contracts across the country? There is no real reason why they should go as a matter of right to printing firms in the Ottawa, Toronto or Montreal areas.

I am able to give
some figures to the hon. member that will indicate that we are increasing the amount of contracts outside of Ontario and Quebec. In Alberta the amount spent this year from April 1 to June 30 was $8,330 compared with $7,746 for the whole of 1958. In British Columbia the amount from April 1 to June 30 this year is $5,156 compared with $3,075 in 1958. In Manitoba the figures are $14,849 and $10,463 in 1958. In other provinces the increases are similar.

I am very pleased that there have been these increases, but while the percentage increase may be great I think the minister will admit that the amounts are still minor in total compared with the rather huge sums that are dispensed in this particular region. I know there are advantages in this particular region but printers beyond the triangle tell me that they would like the opportunity to get in on some of this business. I should like the minister to carry on this policy and push it further. I would
Supply-Secretary of State not like him to get lost in the printing backwoods in this area.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the minister not going to answer some of the statements made by the hon. member for Hull particularly in connection with the contracts involving these higher tenders? Does the minister not think he should tell the committee how it was that in four of these five contracts which were awarded it appears that the contract went to the highest tenderer in each case? (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I am prepared to give certain information contained in one of the letters which have been tabled early in July. It is to be noticed that as detailed specifications were requested, Wilson Jones Limited and Cope-land-Chatterson Ltd., to compare only the two companies involved, were bidding different prices. It will be noted also that the price was adjusted as certain specifications were required. In fact, item 4 of the said letter reads as follows:
(Text):
Under date of March 9, 1959, a requisition for 1,000 binders French was received. Tenders were invited as hereunder.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, this information is taken from a letter sent to me on July 2, 1959, which was part of an order for return. Looking at the bottom of the page, we find that the difference in prices quoted by the two companies was small. In fact, Wilson Jones Limited tried to conform as closely as possible to the specifications of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, and we find that the difference was slight, because its initial price, which was $5.56 per binder, was raised to $7.04, whereas Cope-land-Chatterson submitted a price of $7.84.
However, Mr. Chairman, I should hope that the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron), who spoke at great length after the letter was tabled in the house, would have read this paragraph in the letter that was produced in early July and which reads as follows. (Text):
The order was placed with Wilson Jones Company Limited on the basis that a made-up sample would be accepted by the department prior to production. While the order still stands, the company has not yet been able to satisfy the department that the exact specifications have been met.
(Translation):
Another paragraph reads.

As the department of public printing and stationery has 2,500 paidup back orders on hand, some received as far back as January, from schools, companies, libraries, etc., and in view of the urgent requirement in the Department of Mines

Mr. Chairman, this does not alter what I have said to any extent. I said it was easy for the head of a department, as he is placed so as to be informed, to find all sorts of faults and to explain them as he thinks fit in a letter. That is why I said that it is not so much the minister who is responsible.
If the department was not satisfied with the work of Wilson Jones Limited, it would ask the firm to produce something else to the department's satisfaction. And the minister knows that it is always easy to find a reason for dissatisfaction. That is why I am asking for an investigation so that not only the person who signed the letter but also those who sent in a tender are given an opportunity to state their case, in order to know the difference between the various samples produced for the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. So that does not alter what I said. That is what I said. It may be that officials from the department have a feeling of hatred with regard to some firms and find all sorts of faults. An investigation by the public accounts committee would either justify the government or condemn those responsible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If the minister prefers,
I will speak in French. The minister read two paragraphs from the letter of July 2, 1959. But in reading those two paragraphs I feel the minister has not given sufficient explanation to the house to justify the awarding of a contract such as this one, of four contracts I should say, to the highest bidder. The minister has no doubt other reasons than those mentioned in the letter. He is aware of the situation. He did not himself explain to the house how it is that these four contracts went to the highest bidder.

I would point out to the hon. member for Laurier that the discussions about those binders began in 1956, under another administration. And it is the continuation of those discussions which resulted in what we now see under item 4. As specifications were given-and there again I rely on what I have myself-it is to be noted that Wilson Jones Limited, was quoting a price comparable to that of the firm to which the contract was awarded.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not satisfied with the minister's reply. He said the negotiations for the binders started under a former government. The minister has been asked to indicate when the contracts were let, and the reply given in the minister's return to the house shows that the contracts were let in December 1958, and therefore not under another administration. Also, the other replies indicate that six contracts were let, four of which went to the highest tenderer. I think the minister owes the committee some explanations as to the circumstances.

I can only transmit the information given to me. I have the letter here, and it clearly shows that tenders were called, and certain specifications were given as to the type of binder required. Unfortunately, no bids were made by other companies than Wilson Jones Limited.

The minister has just indicated that in October 1956, authority had been granted to look into the matter with Cope-land-Chatterson Ltd. That is a fact.
(Text):
In October 1956, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys was authorized by this department to work with Copeland-Chatterson Limited in the development of a binder for the Atlas of Canada.
(Translation):
And even if I were to read it all, I could not establish anything else. We are forced to work out the model with Copeland-Chatterson Ltd., they say, on account of the ability of that firm. That does not exclude the right to ask other firms to submit a plan. The proof of that is that when a plan had been established, tenders were called from several firms; in fact, five firms sent in a tender: Wilson Jones Limited; E. G. Thomas; Brown Bros. Limited; Charles Chapman Company; Copeland-Chatterson Ltd. That shows clearly that the department had no intention to do business with one firm but to call for tenders and to grant the contracts, as far as possible, to the lowest tenderer. The explanation that has been given does not justify the awarding of the contract to the highest tenderer. The only way that we could justify the granting of a contract to the highest tenderer would be to call before the public accounts committee the departmental officials involved.
We should call the firms which were invited to tender on the various contracts and have the models produced before the committee so

that we could see for ourselves whether any particular model was so different that it could not have served the purpose.
Therefore I suggest that the only way to satisfy the hon. members and the Canadian public is to call before the committee the highest bidder who was awarded the contract and to submit to the public accounts committee the reasons for that choice. If the authorities were justified it would be easy for them to prove it and if they were not justified I know that the minister and the government would want to tell them exactly how they should proceed in future.

I admit we would get more detailed information from an investigation by the Public Accounts committee. On the other hand I remind the committee that in 1956 Copeland-Chatterson Ltd. were asked to make a model. You then considered that firm to be better qualified than any other to make a model. After that, tenders were invited from other firms, and other firms were asked to make a binder of the most satisfactory model, that is the one proposed in 1956 by the Chatterson firm. That is what I gather from this letter. As tenders were received, it was noted that prices kept getting closer to those of the Copeland-Chatterson firm.

Does the minister admit that it would be more satisfactory to review all this matter? We do not want to blame any one, but there is something wrong somewhere. In fact, the investigating committee found that the highest tender was not the best one. But until then, I am not satisfied, and most of the members, even those who sit on the government side are not either. However, if this whole matter were reviewed, I think everybody would be satisfied.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I make a suggestion to the minister to help him in the solution of this matter?

Supply-Secretary of State it would be better if the hon. minister were to make a statement tomorrow about that.

Oh yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then I ask him this question: Is it a fact that the owner of that printing establishment is the brother-in-law of the minister?
I did not deny that Mr. Gilbert Paquette owned that establishment.

speechtext: No; the question I asked was this. Is the owner of Le Flambeau printing shop, the brother-in-law of the minister?

Mr. Chairman, I would
not like to see the good name of a Mont Laurier printer tarnished because he is my brother-in-law.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

I answer the hon. member for Laurier as tactfully, as respectably and as kindly as he did, and I must tell him that as a printer, whether from Mont Laurier or from anywhere, anybody is allowed, provided he meets the prices established by the printing bureau or the conditions laid down, to put in a bid; he is also allowed to enter into contracts, and I fail to see why

Supply-Secretary of State Mr. Paquette, the owner of the printing concern Le Flambeau, who is my brother-inlaw, would not have the right to get contracts to the amount of $2,000.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have no doubt that what the minister just said is true, that the contract has been awarded under normal circumstances, but what I asked him was simply this to which he did not answer: does he feel it is right, under such circumstances, that a contract be awarded to such a close relative of the minister?
I just answered, perhaps not directly, but I just said to the hon. member for Laurier that I was not even aware that this contract had been granted to Le Flambeau in Mont Laurier.

Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the acting house leader indicate what the government proposes to do tomorrow?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not No. 4.

Of the estimates?

Oh.

Beginning at 9.30 and going right through you would have a clear run of 12 hours to 9.30 in the evening. This is not unusual for the House of Commons. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I make this suggestion. I think, perhaps, there is something in what the hon. member for Skeena says. We have been very co-operative and have sat for quite a long time. May I make this compromise suggestion-that in order to meet the hon. member half way, or almost half way, with regard to his suggestion, we should sit at 10 o'clock. Then, I think, we shall be meeting both the suggestion made by the acting leader of the house and by the hon. member for Skeena.

That is precisely the suggestion which the Minister of Trade and Commerce made. That was the second suggestion and one with which I feel we should not agree.
